docs.title: Evey
docs.text:
Evey is a self-hosted server for your films, series, music and photos. You add your media and the people who watch; Evey adapts playback to your server and to each device on its own.

Install Evey Try the demo

Beta, no numbered release yet Free software, AGPL-3.0 Demo sign-in: demo / demo

Watch in any web browser, on a Chromecast, on Android phones and tablets, and on Android TV. The Android and Android TV apps are in testing and not on Google Play yet. Server: one Docker container on an x86-64 computer or NAS.

The home page: resume playback, then each library. A film page, with its artwork, ratings and credits. The web player. The admin dashboard while two people watch: the picture each one is seeing, and how it is delivered.

docs.title: Run your media server, not its infrastructure
docs.text:
One container, one compose file, no .env to write.

  • Database and search engine included. They are reachable only inside the container, with passwords generated on the first start.
  • File permissions adapted automatically, when possible, so that repairs can write. The server itself never runs as root.
  • Less to size by hand. The graphics card is detected, the transcoding capacity is measured, and the playback mode follows what each device can play.

Bringing your own database or search cluster stays possible: Advanced deployments.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Do as little work as possible

Direct Play sends the file as it is. When the device can play the tracks but not the file's container, MKVGo changes the container without re-encoding the audio and video tracks, and without starting an extra program for each playback; FFmpeg copies the tracks where MKVGo cannot. FFmpeg handles real conversions. MKVGo in Evey

Know what the machine can actually do

An accelerator counts only once a real encode on it succeeds. At a quiet moment the server times test encodes, then sends each stream to the cheapest hardware that proved it can serve it. When room runs short, a new stream gets a lower quality, or moves from a saturated graphics card to the processor; it is refused, with a clear message, only when no capacity is left. Transcoding and server capacity

Third-party code is contained, not trusted

A plugin is analysed before install, gets only the permissions the administrator accepted, and runs as its own process, with no direct network access and capped resources. How strict the sandbox is depends on the host, and the admin panel says which one is active. Security model and plugin sandbox

Find broken media before playback does

Media Health reads your MKV and WebM files and explains what it finds. A repair runs on request, is checked before it replaces the file, keeps the original by default and is journaled. The rest is reported, never rewritten behind your back. Media health

docs.title: See what Evey decided, and why
docs.text:
The dashboard lists every playback: who, on which device, in Direct Play, Remux or Transcode, and what is copied or encoded. In the player, Stream info shows the plan actually served, and why the file was not played as it is.

Remux: the container changes, without re-encoding the video or the audio. "Copied" describes the tracks, not the playback method.

Reading Stream info

docs.title: Apps and extensions
docs.text: A TV signs in from a phone or a computer with Quick Connect, without typing a password. Plugins and themes extend the interface, and the same plugin runs on the web, on Android and on the TV. Apps and devices · Plugins

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Evey is a self-hosted media server. Backend is Go (hexagonal / DDD), frontend is a TypeScript/React monorepo, mobile is React Native / Expo. See DEV.md for setup and deeper internals.

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
Strict ports-and-adapters layout under internal/:

  • internal/domain/<context>/ - pure domain: models, value objects, ports (interfaces). No framework imports.
  • internal/app/<context>/ - application services. Orchestrate ports. IO normally goes through a port; two contexts are deliberate exceptions and reach the network directly: dlna (SSDP / UPnP AVTransport) and loadtest (its own HTTP client).
  • internal/adapters/driven/ - outbound adapters implementing domain ports: postgres, meilisearch, ffmpeg, mkvgo, filesystem, prober, opensubtitles, email, webpush, webhooksender, pluginrunner, metadata, introproviders, search. Two more live here but satisfy an app-layer interface rather than a domain port: itunes and musicbrainz, both app/music.AlbumArtFetcher.
  • internal/adapters/driving/ - inbound adapters: grpcapi (+ grpc-gateway HTTP), http (static, auth middleware, SSE, HLS, plugin iframe assets), pluginhost (gRPC server on a Unix socket, authenticated by peer credentials - the host API that sandboxed plugin subprocesses call back into).
  • internal/pkg/ - shared technical kernel reused across contexts (auth, logger, eventbus, i18n, metrics, tracing, ratelimit, procfork, ssrf, cache, ...). Server configuration lives in internal/config/; generated proto code lives in gen/.

Dependency rule: adapters -> app -> domain. Domain never imports app or adapters. Composition happens in cmd/evey/wire*.go - hand-written wiring, not google/wire: wire.go, wire_infra.go, wire_services.go, wire_adapters.go, wire_events.go, wire_helpers.go.

docs.title: Bounded contexts
docs.text:
Thirty-two context packages live under internal/domain/ and internal/app/: 19 exist in both layers, 2 are domain-only (ratings, shared), 11 are app-only. Collaboration happens partly via domain events published through a shared bus; the app layer also reads a neighbouring context's domain package directly (see Relations).

Context Responsibility user accounts, auth, sessions, preferences library libraries, folders, scan jobs, media index, people, collections, a profile's favorites and thumbs (thumbs have no app service: the rating RPC stores and reads UserRatingRepository as is), trickplay, intro/credits detection media (app only) share links and stream tokens mediarequest user-submitted media requests metadata TMDB / OMDb enrichment, artwork playback streams, progress, remote control, now-playing transcoding ffmpeg jobs, HLS segments subtitle embedded + external + opensubtitles mkv MKV container ops (via mkvgo) music audio-specific playback + tagging photo photo libraries favorite (app only) per-profile favorites; the model and FavoriteRepository live in domain/library playlist user playlists, smart playlists collection (app only) admin-curated collections; its ports live in domain/library ratings (domain only) maps country classifications (CSA, FSK, MPAA, BBFC, ACB) onto one minimum-age axis feed activity feed / discover activity user activity timeline chromecast cast session lifecycle syncplay multi-device sync sessions plugin plugin registry, sandbox tokens, lifecycle notification in-app + webpush notifications webhook outbound webhooks backup DB + config backup/restore config (app only) persisted server settings, written by both the REST and the gRPC entry points dlna (app only) SSDP discovery and UPnP AVTransport control loadtest (app only) simulates HLS viewers against the server's own HTTP stack maintenance (app only) admin-triggered media maintenance: seek-index rebuild, repair journal, undo, audio integrity presence (app only) in-memory, non-persisted registry of who is connected right now qoe (app only) CMCD (CTA-5004) playback telemetry ingest and aggregation demo (app only) the public demo instance (EVEY_DEMO=1): seeds its accounts, libraries and freely licensed media through the product's own services, and resets itself updatecheck (app only) compares the running build with what the registry publishes and tells the administrator; it never updates anything shared (domain only) cross-cutting ports (EventBus, TransactionalUnit, ServerConfigRepository, ShareLinkRepository), typed ids, cursors, stream tokens

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
• library → emits LibraryCreated / LibraryDeleted, LibraryScanStarted / LibraryScanCompleted, MediaItemAdded, MediaItemRemoved, TrickplayGenerated. media.item.added is consumed by notification, metadata (auto-enrich), library itself (trickplay worker + intro detection) and feed (genre-cache invalidation).
  • Search indexing is not event-driven: library.ScanService calls the library.SearchIndex port directly.
  • playback → emits PlaybackStarted / PlaybackStopped. Neither has a dedicated subscriber today; only webhook's "*" catch-all receives them.
  • user → emits UserCreated, which has no subscriber, and user.password.reset_requested, consumed by the email driven adapter.
  • plugin → pluginrunner publishes plugin.error / plugin.started, and app/plugin consumes them for its security dashboard. There is no bridge feeding domain events into plugins: plugins reach the API with scoped JWTs (see ADR-0003). The bus itself is ADR-0010.
  • shared.TransactionalUnit wraps multi-aggregate writes (see ADR-0002).

No package under internal/domain imports another context's domain package - a rule enforced by internal/contractguard/domain_imports_test.go (see Architecture guards). The app layer is not bound by it: 15 app packages import a neighbouring context's domain package today.

docs.title: Typical data flow - "user plays a media"
docs.text:
1. Mobile/web client calls POST /api/v1/playback/start (grpc-gateway route).
  2. internal/adapters/driving/http runs its auth middleware (auth_middleware.go, httpAuthMiddleware), extracts session.
  3. internal/adapters/driving/grpcapi (playback_handler.go) validates proto, calls app/playback.CommandService.StartStream (command/query split, see ADR-0009).
  4. app/playback.CommandService calls domain ports: user.UserRepository, playback.SessionQueryRepo (idempotency + device cap), playback.SessionCommandRepo, then shared.EventBus.Publish(PlaybackStarted).
  5. Driven adapters execute: postgres persists the session inside a shared.TransactionalUnit.Do scope; the in-process bus (internal/pkg/eventbus) dispatches asynchronously.
  6. PlaybackStarted has no dedicated subscriber today: only the webhook "*" catch-all receives it.
  7. Response streams back through grpc-gateway as JSON; progress updates flow over SSE / gRPC streams.

docs.title: Composition root
docs.text: Wire graphs live in cmd/evey/wire.go and its siblings (wire_infra.go, wire_services.go, wire_adapters.go, wire_events.go, wire_helpers.go). Tests bypass adapters by injecting fakes that implement the same domain ports - 20 of the 21 domain packages ship a fakes/ subpackage. See ADR-0001.

docs.title: Architecture guards
docs.text:
The rules above are not documentation-only. internal/contractguard/ holds 54 static tests across 29 files that fail the build when the codebase drifts from them.

The hexagonal rule itself is TestDomainContextsDoNotImportEachOther (ADR-0001), in domain_imports_test.go. It walks internal/domain and enforces exactly this: a context may import internal/domain/shared and its own package tree, nothing else from internal/domain, and never internal/app or internal/adapters. Its scope stops at internal/domain - it says nothing about the app layer.

The rest guard contracts that cross a language or a process boundary, among them:

  • TestNoClientReadOfAFieldTheServerNeverWrites - every proto response field a client reads must be written somewhere on the server.
  • TestRegisteredHandlersGetEveryPortTheyDeclare and TestBootInstallsItsSilentWirings - wiring that would otherwise fail silently.
  • TestPostgresRepositoriesBoundTheirQueries - every Postgres repository bounds its queries with a timeout.
  • TestProcfork_EveryForkGoesThroughCommand - every subprocess fork goes through internal/pkg/procfork.
  • TestEverySortFieldTheAPIAcceptsHasASQLColumn and ...CanBuildACursorValue - sort fields exist both in the SQL column map and in the cursor encoder.
  • TestEveryWebSurfaceReachingAnAdminRPCIsClassified, plus its native counterpart for mobile and TV - any UI surface calling an admin-only RPC decides who sees it.
  • TestEveryAllowedSlotIsMountedOnWebAndMobile and TestPluginBridgeParityWebMobile - plugin UI slot parity across clients.
  • TestImageSubtitleCodecsAgreeAcrossServerAndClients - one list of bitmap subtitle codecs, server and players.
  • TestHandWrittenClientTypesMatchTheEndpointTheyCall - the hand-written mobile/TV response types match the endpoint they call.
  • TestRestartExitCodeAgreesWithTheEntrypoint - the Go exit code and docker/entrypoint.sh agree on what a restart means.
  • i18n guards - server-emitted keys exist in the catalogue, placeholders agree across locales.

docs.text: These four diagrams document Evey at decreasing zoom levels following the C4 model. All diagrams render with Mermaid; no binary assets. Node names are the actual Go package names under internal/. Container names come from docker-compose.yml for evey-server, evey-postgres and evey-caddy; evey-web, evey-meilisearch, evey-mobile and evey-mailcatcher are declared in docker-compose.override.yml and exist in the dev topology only.

Production differs from this dev topology. The install compose declares one service, evey. There is no separate evey-web container (nor the dev-only mailcatcher and Metro bundler): the binary serves the built web UI from /srv, so a reverse proxy forwards everything - UI and API - to it on :9091. Postgres and Meilisearch run inside the same container, supervised by docker/entrypoint.sh: PostgreSQL 17 with its data under /data/postgres, and the Meilisearch binary (Dockerfile, meili-download stage, pinned to 1.12.8) with its index under /data/meili. The repository's own docker-compose.yml keeps separate postgres and caddy services, described in Advanced deployments. See Install and Reverse proxy.

Goroutine notes: - gRPC server (grpc.Server.Serve) and HTTP server (gateway + static) each run in their own goroutines off the main wire-up in cmd/evey. - app/library scan jobs run on a worker pool (one goroutine per active library scan, see library.ScanService). - ffmpeg jobs are forked through internal/pkg/procfork by the driven ffmpeg adapter (ffmpeg.Transcoder.Start), one supervising goroutine per job draining the process stderr. - shared.EventBus dispatches subscribers asynchronously: each subscriber runs in its own goroutine so a slow consumer never blocks publishers. The bus opens no transaction of its own - that is the handler's job. - pluginrunner spawns one subprocess per plugin; iframe plugins live inside the user browser and talk back via signed tokens issued by app/plugin.

docs.title: Plugin sandbox and threat model
docs.text: This page describes what the server does to contain a plugin: the checks at install, the layers at run time, the sandbox modes, and what each still cannot stop. If you are writing a plugin and want to know what you may declare and what will be refused, read Permissions and slots.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Plugins run as separate processes that talk to the server over gRPC on Unix sockets. The server trusts no plugin code by default. The risks it defends against, from the most to the least severe:

  1. Impersonation - a plugin pretends to be another plugin to use its permissions.
  2. Privilege escalation - a plugin escapes its sandbox and runs commands as the server.
  3. Filesystem access - a plugin reads or writes outside its own directory, in particular the server's secrets.
  4. Network exfiltration - a plugin sends data to a host of its choosing.
  5. Resource abuse - mining, fork bombs, memory or disk exhaustion.
  6. Supply chain - obfuscated or compiled code the analysis cannot read.

docs.title: ZIP extraction
docs.text:
Before any file is written:

  • at most 5,000 entries, 100 MB per file, 500 MB uncompressed in total, and a compression ratio of 100:1 above 1 MB uncompressed (decompression bombs);
  • entries whose path leaves the archive (..) are refused;
  • symbolic links are refused;
  • setuid, setgid and sticky bits are removed.

Source: internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/zip.go.

docs.title: Manifest and permissions
docs.text:
The manifest declares the permissions a plugin requests. An unknown permission refuses the install. They are then enforced:

  • subprocess allows child processes. Without it, process creation is refused by the kernel (-deny-fork), and the LD_PRELOAD filter also refuses execve for interpreted plugins.
  • native-binary allows shipping compiled code or archives, which the analysis cannot read.
  • API permissions (api.library, api.user, api.metadata, media.read, media.write, notification.sender...) are checked on every call to the host by PluginPermissionInterceptor.

The full list of permissions is in Permissions and slots.

docs.title: Static analysis
docs.text:
Every file of the package is scanned by pluginrunner.AnalyzePlugin, after a normalisation pass that undoes common obfuscation (aliases, string concatenation, f-strings):

Category Severity Examples shell_exec CRITICAL os.system, subprocess.run, child_process.exec, PHP system()/shell_exec()/proc_open(), preg_replace /e, Ruby backticks, open('\|cmd') network WARNING / CRITICAL requests.get, fetch, reverse and bind shells filesystem WARNING / CRITICAL /etc/passwd, .ssh/, rm -rf, symlink operations obfuscation CRITICAL eval, base64 decoding, hex sequences, __builtins__, base64 -d \| bash privilege CRITICAL setuid, chmod 4777, sudo, signalling PID 1 cryptomining CRITICAL stratum+tcp, xmrig, cryptonight runtime_install CRITICAL pip install, npm install, curl ... \| sh dynamic_import CRITICAL __import__(), importlib.import_module sandbox_escape CRITICAL vm.runIn*, process.binding, new Function, __subclasses__(), __mro__ deserialization CRITICAL / WARNING pickle.loads, marshal.loads, __reduce__; WARNING: yaml.load() without a Loader native_code CRITICAL / WARNING ctypes.CDLL, ffi.Library; WARNING: Go unsafe compiled_binary WARNING, then BLOCK .so, .dll, .exe, .wasm, .jar embedded_archive WARNING, then BLOCK .zip, .tar.gz mime_mismatch treated as CRITICAL an extension that claims an image, with other content suspicious_url WARNING a non-HTTP scheme in a URL literal unvendored_deps WARNING requirements.txt or package.json without vendored modules

A CRITICAL finding or a mime_mismatch refuses the install. compiled_binary and embedded_archive refuse it unless the manifest declares native-binary.

What the analysis cannot guarantee. It works on patterns. It resolves known obfuscation classes (string concatenation into a callable over several steps, builtin lookup by name, Function.constructor escapes), each with a regression fixture in tests/fixtures/plugins/malicious/, but it cannot follow every transformation done at run time (strrev("metsys"), decoding a payload read from a file). It also matches inside comments: a # pip install foo comment triggers runtime_install. The enforcement boundary is the run-time sandbox, not the analysis: a plugin that slips a pattern past it still cannot read the server's data, call a denied system call, exceed its resource limits, or call a host method it has no permission for.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
A package can be signed with cosign. EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY sets what a failed verification does:

Policy Effect off The signature is not checked. warn (default) A failure is recorded and shown to the administrator, without blocking. With no public key configured, nothing is verified. enforce A failure refuses the install or the update.

The public key is given by EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY. Source: internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/cosign.go.

docs.title: Administrator preview
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/admin/plugins/preview runs the analysis without installing. The administrator sees the requested permissions, every finding with its file, line and category, the URLs found in the code, and the SHA256 of the package; the same hash is checked when the install is applied, so the package analysed is the package installed. An update shows the difference in permissions, slots and hosts, and a new permission requires an explicit acknowledgement.

The administrator is the trust boundary for elevated permissions: Evey shows the surface, the administrator accepts or refuses.

docs.title: Filesystem
docs.text: A plugin sees its own directory and its socket directory, and not the server's data. How this is enforced depends on the sandbox mode: a Landlock allowlist, or a bubblewrap mount whitelist. In basic mode on a kernel without Landlock, there is no per-path confinement: the separate user and file permissions are then what protect the server's secrets (below).

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
A plugin has no direct network access, whatever it declares: every IP socket is refused (-deny-inet in landlock and basic, a network namespace in bubblewrap and strict). A plugin with the network permission calls the host's Fetch method over its Unix socket. The host, in internal/adapters/driving/pluginhost/fetch.go:

  • checks the target against the plugin's external_fetch list (exact hosts, case-insensitive);
  • allows only http and https, and only GET and HEAD;
  • connects through an SSRF-safe client (internal/pkg/ssrf) that refuses private, reserved and link-local addresses after DNS resolution, so DNS rebinding and redirects are checked again;
  • adds none of the server's credentials, and caps the response size.

This closes the paths direct egress left open (IP literals such as 169.254.169.254, a plugin's own resolver). What remains: the broker controls where a call goes, not what it carries. See Known limits.

Recommended for operators. The broker moves the SSRF surface to the host. An egress rule on the evey-server container, independent of the code, adds a second wall: drop 169.254.0.0/16 and restrict the internal network to the database and search endpoints.

docs.title: System calls
docs.text:
Two seccomp filters refuse the same dangerous system calls:

  1. The kernel filter, installed by evey-plugin-launcher just before it starts the plugin (seccomp_linux.go). It is inherited by the plugin and its children and also covers compiled, static binaries. A mismatched architecture in a system call kills the process. Applied in landlock and basic.
  2. The LD_PRELOAD filter, sandbox/sandbox.c, loaded into interpreted plugins that do not declare subprocess. It also refuses execve/execveat, and marks the plugin non-dumpable. Applied in landlock, basic and strict. If the library is missing, such a plugin is refused start (plugin.error).

Refused system calls:

Category System calls Debugging ptrace, process_vm_readv, process_vm_writev Signals tgkill, rt_sigqueueinfo, rt_tgsigqueueinfo towards any process but the plugin itself (both filters); kill likewise in the kernel filter, towards any target in the LD_PRELOAD filter; tkill in the kernel filter (the LD_PRELOAD filter allows it towards the plugin itself); pidfd_send_signal, pidfd_getfd (steals a file descriptor). A runtime re-raising a signal or preempting its own threads keeps working. On Landlock ABI 6+, a plugin also cannot signal a process outside its sandbox Mounts mount, umount2, pivot_root, chroot Namespaces unshare, setns Kernel modules init_module, finit_module, delete_module BPF, perf bpf, perf_event_open Hardware I/O ioperm, iopl (x86-64 only, where they exist) Swap swapon, swapoff System control syslog, reboot, settimeofday, clock_settime, clock_adjtime, adjtimex Kexec kexec_load, kexec_file_load Kernel exploit primitives io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter, io_uring_register, userfaultfd Identity setuid, setgid, setreuid, setregid, setresuid, setresgid, capset Keyring add_key, request_key, keyctl

For a plugin without subprocess, the kernel also refuses process creation (fork, vfork, clone without CLONE_THREAD); threads keep working.

This is a denylist: open, read, write, mmap, Unix socket and connect stay allowed. Paths are confined by the filesystem layer, not by seccomp. In bubblewrap the launcher is not used: a static binary gets no seccomp filter there, and is contained by the namespaces and the mount whitelist.

docs.title: A separate user
docs.text:
A plugin can run as user 1001 (evey-plugin), distinct from the server (1000), so the server's secrets are unreadable to it by file permissions alone. EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION controls it:

  • auto (default): only when the sandbox resolves to basic, the one case where file permissions are the only wall around the secrets;
  • on: always, as an extra layer;
  • off: never.

The switch is made by the launcher, which holds cap_setuid; the server itself runs without privileges or capabilities. The launcher refuses any target below 1000. If it cannot switch, a plugin in basic is refused (the user is the only wall there), while in landlock it runs as the server's user with a warning. In bubblewrap and strict, the user namespace plays this role.

When active, the signing key (0600) and the backups (0700 directory, 0600 files) are owner-only at run time, which holds even on a bind-mounted /data. All plugins share user 1001: they are isolated from each other by the filesystem layer, not by the user.

docs.title: Host socket authentication
docs.text: Each plugin has its own socket, /tmp/evey/plugins/<plugin_id>/host.sock, served by its own gRPC server. On every call, the server reads the caller's PID from the kernel (SO_PEERCRED, which user space cannot forge) and compares it with the PID recorded when the plugin started. The plugin's identity comes from the socket, never from a header. A plugin therefore cannot impersonate another, call another plugin's socket, or route calls through a child process.

docs.title: Resource limits
docs.text:
A monitor in user space (cgroups are unavailable in an unprivileged container) reads /proc/<pid> every 2 seconds or so and stops a plugin that exceeds a limit:

  • memory (RSS), 256 MiB by default;
  • processes and threads, 64 by default;
  • disk used by its directory, 100 MiB by default, checked every 30 seconds;
  • CPU priority, nice 10 by default, applied at start.

The limits are set per plugin in Admin → Plugins. See ADR-0013.

docs.title: Interface isolation
docs.text: A plugin's interface runs in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">, without same-origin access, forms or popups, under a Content-Security-Policy that allows connections only to its external_fetch hosts. The bridge limits what it can ask of the page: toast at most 3 per second, 200 characters, no HTML; navigate accepts only /home, /library, /media, /player, /settings and /search; resize between 50 and 800 px. Slots are checked at install and again at render.

docs.title: Server hardening
docs.text: At startup the server marks itself non-dumpable (PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0, hardening_linux.go): a process running as the same user cannot read its memory or environment through /proc, which protects the signing key in memory and the database and search passwords, even on a kernel without Landlock.

docs.title: Crash notification
docs.text: The runner publishes a plugin.error event when the sandbox library is missing for a plugin that needs it, or when a plugin exits with an error. The notification service forwards it to the administrator through the configured channels. A PID mismatch on a host socket is logged as a warning.

docs.title: Sandbox modes
docs.text: The mode selects how the filesystem and the network are confined. EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE sets the initial value (default auto); it can be changed in Admin → Plugins. The runner applies it in applySandbox. In every mode: no direct IP egress, the resource monitor, and the host socket authentication.

docs.title: auto (default)
docs.text: Resolves, once at the first plugin start, to the strongest mode the host supports: landlock, then bubblewrap, then basic. Landlock comes first because it needs no privilege and runs under Docker's default security profile. bubblewrap is chosen only when Landlock is absent and a test sandbox actually builds (ProbeSandbox), which in practice means bare metal or a privileged container. The resolved mode is logged, and shown on the Host sandbox line of Admin → Plugins → Security Dashboard.

docs.title: landlock
docs.text:
• Filesystem: a Landlock allowlist applied by the launcher. System directories (/usr, /lib, /lib64, /bin, /sbin, /etc, /app) read-only; of /dev, only null, zero, full, random and urandom, so graphics card nodes and the server's terminal stay out of reach; the plugin's directory and socket directory read-write; everything else, including /data and other plugins, denied. A plugin granted hardware.gpu gets its render node as the one exception.
  • Network: -restrict-net and -deny-inet; egress only through Fetch.
  • System calls: the kernel filter and the LD_PRELOAD filter.
  • Requires: a kernel 5.13 or newer with Landlock in the active LSM list, and the launcher (both are the case on the official image with a recent host). An explicit landlock refuses to start a plugin it cannot confine.

docs.title: bubblewrap
docs.text:
• Filesystem and processes: six unshared namespaces (user, pid, uts, ipc, cgroup, net) and a mount whitelist; nothing else exists inside.
Path Access /usr, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /lib64 read-only /etc/ssl, /etc/ca-certificates, /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/{alpine,os}-release read-only (never /etc as a whole: no passwd, shadow, ssh) the plugin's directory, its socket directory read-write /proc its own mount /dev a minimal synthetic set (null, zero, random, urandom, tty, pts) /tmp an empty tmpfs

/data, /var, /home, /root, /run and other plugins' directories do not exist inside. A canary plugin (tests/fixtures/plugins/canary-sandbox-runtime/) checks this layout against a running stack. Source: buildBwrapCmd in internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/runner_bwrap.go. - Network: the network namespace, for every plugin. - System calls: no seccomp filter; the namespaces provide the isolation. - Requires: the bwrap binary and the mount/unshare system calls. In Docker that needs a relaxed security profile, so this is effectively a bare-metal mode.

docs.title: strict
docs.text: bubblewrap plus the LD_PRELOAD filter (interpreted plugins only).

docs.title: basic
docs.text: The last resort of auto: the separate user, the kernel filter, the LD_PRELOAD filter, -deny-inet, and Landlock if the kernel has it. On a kernel without Landlock there is no per-path confinement: a plugin can read non-sensitive world-readable files and see the process list. The server's secrets stay protected by the separate user and PR_SET_DUMPABLE, the network is cut, and dangerous system calls are refused, compiled binaries included.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Layer landlock basic bubblewrap strict Filesystem Landlock allowlist none without Landlock (file permissions only) mount whitelist mount whitelist Network -restrict-net + -deny-inet -deny-inet network namespace network namespace Kernel seccomp (static binaries too) yes yes no no LD_PRELOAD seccomp (interpreted plugins without subprocess) yes yes no yes Separate user with on yes (auto) user namespace user namespace Resource limits yes yes yes yes Deployment What you get Docker on a recent kernel (auto gives landlock) Per-path confinement, no direct egress, dangerous system calls refused including static binaries. The normal case. Docker on an old kernel without Landlock, e.g. an old NAS (auto gives basic) Secrets protected and network cut, but world-readable files visible. See Plugin sandbox setup. Bare metal (auto gives bubblewrap) The strongest filesystem and process isolation, without a seccomp filter for static binaries.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE auto auto, landlock, bubblewrap, strict or basic. Also editable in Admin → Plugins. EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION auto auto, on or off. Incompatible with no_new_privs on the container. EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY warn off, warn or enforce. EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY none The key signatures are checked against.

The official image ships evey-plugin-launcher (Landlock and the kernel filter) and bubblewrap. bubblewrap also needs unprivileged user namespaces on the host. Which setup fits which machine, in plain terms: Plugin sandbox setup.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text: Limit Impact What limits it today No per-path confinement in basic on a kernel without Landlock A plugin can read non-sensitive world-readable files and other plugins' directories Secrets protected by the separate user and PR_SET_DUMPABLE; auto prefers Landlock or bubblewrap All plugins share user 1001 A plugin can signal its siblings (signalling the server is refused) PR_SET_DUMPABLE blocks reading other processes through /proc; Landlock and bubblewrap isolate plugin directories Seccomp is a denylist File and Unix socket calls stay allowed Paths are confined by Landlock or bubblewrap; IP sockets are refused The broker moves the SSRF surface to the host A flaw in the broker's validation could reach an internal address Allowlist and SSRF-safe client in Go; an egress rule on the container as an independent layer The broker controls where a call goes, not what it carries Data can leave towards a host on the plugin's list Allow only hosts you trust with that data The analysis works on patterns Deliberate obfuscation can hide code Administrator preview; the sandbox, not the analysis, is the boundary LD_PRELOAD only covers dynamic, interpreted plugins A static binary in basic without the launcher escapes it The official image always ships the launcher, whose kernel filter covers static binaries

docs.title: Network exposure (outside the plugin threat model)
docs.text:
Two invariants govern who can reach the server at all:

  • Only the HTTP port is meant to be published. The gRPC port (EVEY_SERVER_PORT, default 9090) is an internal transport whose only client is the HTTP gateway in the same process; the HTTP API is that port plus one. gRPC binds to loopback by default (EVEY_GRPC_BIND=127.0.0.1) because the remote-access gate is HTTP middleware and does not cover it. Widening the bind logs a warning; firewalling it is then the operator's job.
  • The remote-access gate decides from the one client address validated at the trusted proxy boundary, never from a request header. A client cannot claim 127.0.0.1 through X-Forwarded-For, and a request that never crossed that boundary counts as remote. This is a deployment control, not authentication.

See Remote access and HTTPS and the Configuration reference.

docs.title: What the logs may contain
docs.text: The server log feeds Logs & Debug, bug reports and backups, so credentials are scrubbed when a line is written (internal/pkg/logger/redact.go): an attribute whose key names a secret (authorization, token, api_key, password, pin, secret...) is replaced whole, and any string carrying a bearer token, a JWT or a secret=value pair is scrubbed. The log routes apply the same rule to older lines on the way out. For code: never log a non-secret value under a secret key name (it will be masked), and add a new kind of credential to that list before it is ever logged.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Report privately, never in a public issue: security@eveyproject.org, the address of the repository's security policy. It covers plugin authentication, permissions and sandbox escapes like anything else. Do not test against Evey instances that are not yours.

docs.title: What a backup contains
docs.text:
A backup is a copy of the database: accounts, profiles, libraries and their metadata, watch history and resume points, collections and playlists, settings, plugin records, webhooks and audit logs. It is a .tar.gz holding the SQL dump and a manifest with the dump's SHA256.

It does not contain:

  • your media files;
  • the transcoding cache (regenerated on demand);
  • the search index (rebuilt from the database);
  • the keys kept in ./evey-data: jwt.key, which signs sessions, and the keys folder (database password, search key);
  • the installed plugin files.

A database backup therefore restores Evey's state on the same installation. To be able to rebuild a machine, keep a copy of the whole ./evey-data folder as well: the database backups are inside it, in ./evey-data/backups.

docs.title: Scheduled backups
docs.text:
Admin → Database Backup → Schedule: a cron expression (for example 0 3 * * *, every day at 3 AM) and a retention in days. Backups older than the retention are deleted after each scheduled run. Run now makes one immediately.

A backup every day at 3 AM, kept 30 days.

The server also dumps the database on its own before applying a migration during an update, whatever the schedule (see below).

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text:
Admin → Database Backup lists the backups and restores one, or restores from a file you upload. Restoring replaces the current database.

A backup can only be restored on a server with the same database schema: the server checks the checksum and the schema version first, and refuses a backup taken by a version with a different schema instead of loading it. To go back to an older version with its data, see Going back below.

When the server does not start any more, the command line restores the dumps taken before a migration (pre-migration-*.sql.gz), not the .tar.gz backups of this panel: see Recovery.

docs.title: Updating Evey
docs.text:
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f evey

That is the whole update. When the new version needs to change the database, it first writes a dump to ./evey-data/backups/pre-migration-*, then applies the migrations while starting; a large catalogue can take a few minutes, and the container reports healthy once it serves again. Evey checks every 6 hours whether a newer image is published and says so in the admin panel; it never updates itself.

Pin what you run. During the beta there is no numbered release and no latest tag; the branch tag beta-0.0.1 moves with every change. For a server you rely on, put an immutable sha-<commit> tag on the image: line, so that two pulls a day apart run the same code. Once releases exist, latest will follow the most recent stable one, and a release tag (0.2.0) will pin it.

Which version is running. docker exec evey-server evey version prints the version and the commit of the running binary.

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
Put the previous tag on the image: line and run docker compose up -d. If the newer version had migrated the database, restore its pre-migration dump first: docker exec evey-server evey admin rollback prints the exact steps with the dump's path.

Image tags, runtime variants and GPU flavours are described in Advanced deployments.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
Two places, one rule. What must exist before the server starts (secrets, storage, the public address, reverse-proxy facts) goes in the compose file. What an administrator tunes afterwards (languages, transcoding limits, hardware acceleration, schedules, plugin limits) lives in the admin panel, is stored in the database, survives a container update, and mostly applies without a restart. For a setting that exists in both places, an environment variable only seeds the first start: the value saved in the panel wins.

The variables, by topic:

Page Covers Server and network Public address, ports, reverse proxy, remote access, request limits, container user Database and search Embedded or external Postgres and Meilisearch Accounts and sign-in Session lifetimes, signing key, single sign-on Libraries and metadata Scanning, metadata keys, intro detection Transcoding and hardware Graphics card, capacity, quality limits, cache, calibration clip Playback delivery and downloads Stream packaging switches, prepared downloads, player skip buttons Background work Background passes and their pacing Plugins and sandbox Sandbox mode, separate user, resource limits, signatures E-mail and notifications SMTP, browser push keys Backups, logs and monitoring Backups, log, history retention, metrics and tracing

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
The embedded Postgres and Meilisearch generate their secrets on the first start, in ./evey-data/keys (postgres.password, meili.key, mode 0600). The server reads them through EVEY_DB_PASSWORD_FILE and MEILI_MASTER_KEY_FILE, set in the image, which is also why evey admin commands need no password. Set EVEY_DB_PASSWORD or MEILI_MASTER_KEY only for an external database or search engine; an explicit value wins over the file.

A TMDB key is built in. EVEY_TMDB_API_KEY seeds your own; the key set in Admin → Server Config → API Keys wins over it.

docs.title: Variables you do not need
docs.text:
Lines often carried over from older setups, and why they change nothing:

Line Why it is unnecessary EVEY_LOG_DIR, EVEY_TRANSCODING_CACHE_DIR, EVEY_TRICKPLAY_CACHE_DIR The image already sets these to /data/logs, /cache/transcode, /data/trickplay. Repeating them changes nothing. EVEY_FORWARDED_PROTO Deprecated - derived from the scheme of EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL. Setting it only logs a deprecation warning. EVEY_KEYFRAME_BACKFILL=on Anything other than off enables it, including absent. LIBVA_DRIVER_NAME libva picks the driver from the GPU's PCI id. Force it only if your card needs a driver libva does not choose (verify with docker exec evey-server vainfo). EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE auto picks the strongest confinement your host supports. Set it explicitly only when you want a fail-closed guarantee - landlock refuses to run a plugin it cannot confine, where auto degrades with a warning. a group_add for /dev/dri/card0 Evey only ever opens renderD128. Check with ls -ln /dev/dri and add that group alone.

docs.title: File ownership (PUID and PGID)
docs.text:
Default: automatic. When PUID/PGID are not set, the entrypoint looks at the owner of your /media* mounts at startup and runs the server as that user, so the features that write into your library (the seek-index repair rebuilds files in place) work out of the box - no chown, no configuration. The startup log tells you what was picked:

evey: media mounts owned by 1026:100 (detected on /media) - running the
server as that user so write features (seek-index repair) work out of the box

Media mounts owned by different users are handled best-effort: the server adopts the user owning the most mounts and joins the other mounts' groups as supplementary groups, so repairs on those mounts work when their files are group-writable (the startup warning lists which mounts may still refuse writes). Auto-detection only steps aside entirely (falls back to 1000:1000 with a warning) when every media mount is owned by root or by the reserved uid 1001 - chown your media to a regular user, or set PUID/PGID explicitly:

.env
PUID=1026   # run the server as this user id  (host: `id -u <media-owner>`)
PGID=100    # ...and this group id

Explicit values always win over detection.

How it works: the container starts as root just long enough to re-map its internal user (and re-own Evey's own state directories /data, /cache - never your media mounts), then drops privileges. Supplementary groups granted via compose group_add: (e.g. your host's render group for /dev/dri hardware transcoding) are preserved across the drop. The server process itself never runs as root.

Zero-root alternative: if even that transient root is unacceptable to you, set user: "UID:GID" on the service in your compose file instead. The entrypoint detects the non-root start and skips the re-map (including the media-owner detection) - you then own keeping ./evey-data writable by that UID yourself.

Notes: - PUID=1001 is refused: it is the internal evey-plugin user, kept distinct so plugins can never share the server's identity. - Media is mounted read-write by default so repairs work natively; append :ro to the media volume if you prefer a read-only library (repairs will then fail with a clear error).

docs.title: Variables the server does not read
docs.text:
Some variables appear in compose files without being read by the server:

  • EVEY_HTTP_PORT, EVEY_DOMAIN, MEDIA_DIR: used by the repository's own docker-compose.yml (published port, the bundled Caddy's domain, the media path), not by Evey. EVEY_VERSION is the image tag there; the server only shows it on /healthz when its binary carries no version.
  • EVEY_WEB_DIR (/srv, where the web interface files are), and EVEY_DB_PASSWORD_FILE, MEILI_MASTER_KEY_FILE, EVEY_IMAGE_REPO, EVEY_IMAGE_RUNTIMES: match the image's layout. Changing them is not supported.
  • EVEY_SUPERVISED, EVEY_COMPANION_PIDS, EVEY_RESTART_EXIT_CODE, EVEY_LAUNCHER_BIN, EVEY_PLUGIN_LAUNCHER: set by the entrypoint and the plugin launcher for their own use.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Evey is developed in the open, and the documents written for the people who work on its code live with the code, on GitHub, rather than on this site. This page points at them.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: You want to Read Build and run Evey from source DEV.md Know the rules of a contribution: branches, commits, tests, the licence agreement CONTRIBUTING.md Find your way in the code in half an hour Codebase map Understand the layering and the bounded contexts Architecture Follow the conventions the code already uses Code conventions Work on the interface Frontend design system Know why a structural choice was made Architecture decisions Cut a release Release runbook

docs.title: Why a decision record, and where
docs.text: Every structural choice - the hexagonal layout, how plugin tokens are scoped, why the install is a single compose file, how one playback plan decides for every client - has an architecture decision record: the context, the options that were weighed, what was chosen and what it costs. They are kept in the repository, next to the code they explain, and are the place to start before proposing to change one of those choices.

docs.title: Before you open a pull request
docs.text:
• make pre-push is the gate: it runs the CI's checks locally (vet, vulnerability scan, build, unit tests with -race, frontend, lint, architecture guards). It does not build the Docker image or the Android apps: after touching the Dockerfile or Kotlin code, build them yourself.
  • Tests are expected for new behaviour and for every bug fix.
  • External contributions need a one-time acceptance of the contributor licence agreement: Evey is AGPL-3.0-or-later and is also offered under a commercial licence. You keep the copyright on your work.

Security issues are not reported in public: write to security@eveyproject.org (see SECURITY.md).

docs.title: Bare-Metal Deployment (no Docker)
docs.text:
Running Evey directly on a host (systemd, an init script, or by hand) instead of the Docker image. The Docker image is the recommended path - it ships the plugin sandbox, hardening, and runtimes pre-wired. Going bare metal means you reproduce that posture: the right binaries side by side, a dedicated non-root user, the sandbox backend your kernel supports, and owner-only secret directories. This page is the step-by-step for that.

If you only want the easy install, stop here and use installation.md.

docs.title: Binaries (build from source)
docs.text:
Build both Go binaries and place them in the same directory. The plugin runner locates the launcher by checking $EVEY_PLUGIN_LAUNCHER first, then next to its own executable (os.Executable()), then $PATH - so keeping them adjacent is the simplest correct layout.

# from the repo root
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w -X main.version=$(git describe --tags --always) -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -o evey ./cmd/evey
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w"                                        -o evey-plugin-launcher ./cmd/evey-plugin-launcher

# install side by side, e.g.:
sudo install -m 0755 evey evey-plugin-launcher /opt/evey/

# optional: shell completion and the manual page, both printed by the binary
/opt/evey/evey completion bash | sudo tee /etc/bash_completion.d/evey >/dev/null
/opt/evey/evey man | sudo tee /usr/local/share/man/man1/evey.1 >/dev/null

Lookup order in launcherPath() (internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/runner_landlock.go):

  1. $EVEY_PLUGIN_LAUNCHER (must be an executable file) - explicit override.
  2. evey-plugin-launcher in the same directory as the running evey binary.
  3. evey-plugin-launcher somewhere on $PATH.

docs.title: The LD_PRELOAD seccomp shim
docs.text:
Build the libevey-sandbox.so shim (a small C file; needs a C compiler):

gcc -shared -fPIC -nostartfiles -o libevey-sandbox.so sandbox/sandbox.c
sudo install -m 0644 libevey-sandbox.so /app/libevey-sandbox.so

The runner looks for it at the hardcoded path /app/libevey-sandbox.so (sandboxLibPath in runner.go). If it is absent, plugins refuse to start (fail-closed) - unless you run in dev mode. This shim adds a seccomp denylist for dynamically-linked plugins and is layered on top of Landlock/bubblewrap.

The Docker image keeps the open-source binaries, SDK, and this shim under /app (no secrets there). On bare metal you can either mirror that path (/app/libevey-sandbox.so) or symlink it.

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
Install whatever your plugins' entrypoint: invokes. The runner recognises these interpreters (knownInterpreters in runner_start.go): python3, python, node, php, ruby, perl, lua, bash, sh. At minimum:

  • python3 - the majority of community plugins.
  • node, php, ruby, lua - only if your plugins use them.

Plus the core runtime dependencies:

  • ffmpeg (transcoding; the image also bundles VAAPI drivers + chromaprint for intro detection).
  • PostgreSQL (server + a database).
  • Meilisearch (search index; or run it embedded via the official binary).
  • bwrap (bubblewrap) - only if you intend to use the bubblewrap sandbox backend (see below).
  • libcap (setcap) - to grant the file capability described in §4.

docs.title: 2. Run as a dedicated non-root user
docs.text:
Never run the server as root. Create a group and two unprivileged users, as the Docker image does; plugins are dropped to UID 1001 (pluginUID in pluginhost/host_server.go):

sudo groupadd --gid 1000 evey
sudo useradd --system --uid 1000 --gid evey --shell /usr/sbin/nologin evey
sudo useradd --system --uid 1001 --gid evey --shell /usr/sbin/nologin evey-plugin

The group's id matters: the launcher drops a plugin to UID 1001 and to the server's own group, and refuses any id below 1000. A group created by useradd --system alone gets a system id below 1000, and plugins in basic mode are then refused.

  • evey (UID 1000) runs the server.
  • evey-plugin (UID 1001) is the UID plugins are dropped to (by the launcher when uid separation is active), so a compromised plugin lands as a different, unprivileged user that cannot read the server's secrets by plain filesystem permissions. See §4.

The server marks itself non-dumpable at startup (PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0, cmd/evey/hardening_linux.go) so a co-resident plugin can't scrape /proc/<server-pid>/{mem,environ}.

docs.title: 3. Pick the sandbox backend for your kernel
docs.text: Set EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE. auto (the default) resolves landlock → bubblewrap → basic and picks the strongest your host supports (resolveAutoMode() in runner_landlock.go). Choose explicitly if you want fail-closed behaviour.

docs.title: Landlock (recommended)
docs.text:
A per-path filesystem allowlist (plugins see only their own dir + socket dir, never your data/secrets) plus a Landlock v4 TCP-egress filter. Needs no privilege, no mount, no namespaces - the launcher applies it to itself, then execves the plugin.

Kernel requirement - Landlock must be both compiled in and in the active LSM list. The runner's landlockAvailable() (landlock_probe_linux.go) probes landlock_create_ruleset(VERSION); it returns an errno when the syscall is absent (kernel <5.13) or when Landlock is not in the active LSM list. Verify:

uname -r                              # want >= 5.13
cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm          # must include "landlock"

If landlock is missing from that list, enable it on the kernel command line and reboot (the exact list varies per distro - keep the existing entries and append landlock):

# e.g. in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX:
lsm=lockdown,capability,yama,apparmor,bpf,landlock

Then:

EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=landlock    # explicit + fail-closed (refuses a plugin if Landlock can't be enforced)
# or leave it on the default:
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=auto        # resolves to landlock when available

landlock mode passes -require-landlock to the launcher, which exits non-zero rather than running a plugin unconfined if Landlock isn't enforced.

docs.title: bubblewrap
docs.text:
If you can't get Landlock, install the bwrap binary. bubblewrap puts each plugin in user/pid/uts/ipc/(net) namespaces with a mount whitelist. It needs unprivileged user namespaces enabled and the mount syscall available - true on most bare-metal Linux, but blocked inside a non-privileged Docker container (which is exactly why Landlock is the container default). auto only selects bubblewrap when Landlock is absent and a throwaway bwrap probe actually succeeds (ProbeSandbox / sandbox_probe.go).

EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=bubblewrap  # bwrap namespaces
# or:
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=strict      # bubblewrap + the LD_PRELOAD seccomp shim

Sanity-check that the host actually permits the namespace+mount setup:

bwrap --unshare-user --unshare-net --ro-bind / / /bin/true && echo "bwrap OK"

docs.title: basic (last resort)
docs.text:
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=basic - UID drop + the LD_PRELOAD seccomp shim, and the launcher still installs the kernel seccomp denylist and best-effort Landlock if present. There is no per-path filesystem confinement: a plugin runs at UID 1001 with seccomp only. Use this only on old/locked-down kernels where neither Landlock nor bubblewrap is available, and lean on the UID separation in §4 to protect secrets.

A plugin granted the subprocess permission requires the launcher, even in basic mode. The LD_PRELOAD shim does not survive an exec of a child process, so it cannot confine a plugin allowed to spawn subprocesses - only the launcher's kernel seccomp (installed right before exec and inherited across it) does. If evey-plugin-launcher is missing (see §1), such a plugin refuses to start in production (fail-closed) rather than running unconfined. Plugins without that permission fall back to the LD_PRELOAD shim as documented above.

docs.title: 4. UID separation (protect secrets without root)
docs.text:
UID separation runs each plugin under a separate user (UID 1001, evey-plugin), distinct from the server (UID 1000), so a plugin can't read the server's jwt.key, backups or logs by plain filesystem permissions (DAC). It matters most in basic mode (no Landlock path confinement); under Landlock or bubblewrap the filesystem is already walled off, so it's redundant there.

Controlled by EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION (auto | on | off, default auto):

  • auto - enable only when the sandbox resolves to basic. On a modern bare-metal kernel (Landlock) it stays off, by design.
  • on - always, even under Landlock/bubblewrap (an extra independent layer).
  • off - never.

The drop is done by the launcher, not the server. The server stays non-root with no capabilities; the small evey-plugin-launcher binary carries a single file capability and setuids itself to 1001 just before exec'ing the plugin:

sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep /opt/evey/evey-plugin-launcher

This keeps the server fully unprivileged - a server RCE can't setuid(0) because the server holds no caps; only the tiny, no-input launcher does (and it refuses any target UID below 1000). If the launcher can't drop (capability missing, or no_new_privs set), a plugin in basic mode is refused - the UID is its only secret wall there; under Landlock it logs a warning and runs at the server's UID.

Incompatible with no_new_privs. If you launch the server with no-new-privileges (or systemd NoNewPrivileges=yes), the file capability is ignored on exec: plugins are refused in basic mode, and under Landlock uid separation degrades to same-UID (with a warning). Pick one.

If the server runs as root instead (not recommended), it drops plugins to 1001 directly and the launcher capability isn't needed.

See the plain-language guide for the per-scenario picture: plugins/sandbox-deployment.md.

docs.title: 5. Secret file permissions
docs.text:
Mirror what the Docker image does (Dockerfile): keep the secret-bearing directories owner-only so a plugin dropped to UID 1001 can't read them via plain DAC, even without Landlock.

sudo chown -R evey:evey /var/lib/evey
# The SERVER owns plugins/ (it extracts installs there); group evey - which
# evey-plugin belongs to - only reads/execs the installed files:
sudo chmod 750 /var/lib/evey/plugins
# owner-only (no group/other) on the secret dirs:
sudo chmod 700 /var/lib/evey/keys /var/lib/evey/logs /var/lib/evey/backups
# the JWT signing key itself:
sudo chmod 600 /var/lib/evey/jwt.key      # (auto-generated 0600 on first boot)

(Adjust paths to wherever you point EVEY_*_DIR / EVEY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH.)

docs.title: 6. Environment & config
docs.text:
All runtime config is via EVEY_* environment variables. Set the database, search, storage paths, JWT key path, and reverse-proxy vars the same way the Docker deployment does - see configuration.md for the full table and installation.md for the database/search/reverse-proxy walkthrough. Don't duplicate the table here. Notes specific to bare metal:

  • Point EVEY_DB_HOST / EVEY_MEILI_URL at your local PostgreSQL / Meilisearch.
  • The server still serves plain HTTP - put a reverse proxy in front for TLS (an https:// External URL and the proxy in Trusted proxies, in Admin → Remote Access, or EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL and EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES). See reverse-proxy.md.
  • The server opens TWO ports, and only one of them may be exposed. EVEY_SERVER_PORT (default 9090) is the native gRPC listener; the HTTP API your clients and reverse proxy talk to is that port plus one (9091). Point your reverse proxy and your firewall at the HTTP port only. The gRPC port is an internal transport: the remote-access network gate, which decides whether clients outside your LAN may connect at all, is wired into the HTTP chain and does not cover the gRPC listener. Because of that, the gRPC listener binds to loopback only by default (EVEY_GRPC_BIND=127.0.0.1), so a bare-metal run cannot expose it by accident. If you have a reason to publish it - a native gRPC client on another host - set EVEY_GRPC_BIND=0.0.0.0; the server warns at boot that the gate does not apply to it, and firewalling it is then on you.
  • Migrations run automatically at startup; no separate migrate step.
  • The plugin resource caps (EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB, _PIDS_MAX, _DISK_MAX_MB, _CPU_NICE) and the sandbox mode are admin-editable at runtime from Admin → Plugins; the env values are just the initial defaults.

docs.title: 7. Verify your sandbox
docs.text:
The server logs the resolved sandbox backend. After the first plugin starts, check the server log:

  • auto resolution (logged once): plugin sandbox auto-detection complete selected_mode=landlock (or bubblewrap / basic).
  • per-plugin (every plugin start): plugin sandbox applied sandbox_mode=landlock plugin_id=...
  • fell back to basic (a warning you do not want to see if you expected Landlock): plugin sandbox auto-detection fell back to basic mode: no per-path filesystem isolation available … - means neither Landlock nor a working bwrap was found. Re-check §3.

Confirm the kernel pieces independently:

cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm          # Landlock active? (should list "landlock")
grep Seccomp: /proc/<plugin-pid>/status   # 2 = filter mode active on a running plugin

A Seccomp: 2 line on a live plugin process confirms the kernel seccomp filter is installed. If you pinned EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=landlock and Landlock isn't enforced, the plugin refuses to start - that's the fail-closed contract working as intended.

For everything else (backups, updates, recovery CLI, troubleshooting) the Docker-oriented sections of installation.md apply equally - the evey admin subcommands and backup mechanics are the same binary.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text: The principles below explain why Evey behaves as it does. Each is a constraint the code follows, with the pages and decision records where it shows. When two of them conflict, the earlier one in this list wins.

docs.title: 1. Access is refused when it cannot be checked
docs.text:
Where a decision grants access, an error resolves to the most restrictive answer. A profile whose parental settings cannot be read gets no content; a plugin whose code cannot be analysed is not installed; remote access follows an explicit choice once one was made, and says loudly when it refuses everyone. Remote access and authentication are separate: the first is a deployment choice, the second is what protects the library.

See Users, profiles and parental control, Remote access and HTTPS, ADR-0026.

docs.title: 2. Third-party code is contained, not trusted
docs.text:
A plugin gets the permissions its manifest declares and nothing else, is analysed before installation, runs in a sandbox with no direct network access, and holds a token that is denied by default. What the sandbox still cannot prevent is written down rather than implied.

See Security model and plugin sandbox, ADR-0012, ADR-0014.

docs.title: 3. The original is delivered whenever it can be
docs.text:
The preferred outcome is the file as it is, then the same tracks in another container, then a transcode of only the tracks that need it. Quality is not something the viewer has to choose before playing: the server keeps the source's quality unless a real constraint (the device, the connection, a limit) prevents it.

See How playback is decided.

docs.title: 4. Decisions rest on what was proved, not on names
docs.text:
A player's capabilities come from what its device reports, not from a list of known devices. A graphics card is used for what it passed during measurement, not for what its model should support. When a capability cannot be proved, the server takes the conservative answer: an unknown cast receiver gets the capabilities of the oldest one, and pixel formats players do not yet report follow a fixed compatibility rule. Assuming too much gives a black screen or wrong colours; assuming too little costs a transcode.

See Casting, Hardware acceleration, ADR-0029.

docs.title: 5. One playback, one decision
docs.text:
A playback is decided once, when it starts, and every manifest and segment of the session is served from that decision. The player never receives segments from two encodings, and what Stream info reports is derived from the same serving plan the playback pipeline uses, checked by tests in both directions.

See ADR-0030, ADR-0024.

docs.title: 6. The server sizes itself to the machine
docs.text:
The server measures how much it can transcode and admits no more: a small machine plays fewer transcoded streams, rather than playing all of them badly. Playback comes first; background work pauses while someone watches. The same image runs on a NAS and on a server with several graphics cards.

See Transcoding and server capacity, Background work and server load.

docs.title: 7. Few settings, each in one place
docs.text:
What must exist before the server starts (storage, secrets, the public address) is in the compose file; everything that can change later is in the admin panel, stored in the database, and applies without a restart wherever nothing requires it. Detection and measurement replace settings wherever they can: an installation is one compose file, libraries and users.

See Install, Configuration reference, ADR-0028.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text: Structural choices are recorded as architecture decision records, with the context, the options weighed and the consequences. They are kept with the code: docs/adr.

docs.title: Languages & Accessibility
docs.text: An honest account of where Evey stands on internationalization (i18n) and accessibility (a11y): what works, how it works, and what doesn't yet. This is a self-hosted project built and maintained by one person - treat a11y in particular as best-effort, not certified.

docs.title: What is and isn't translated
docs.text:
• Translated: the UI chrome - buttons, menus, settings, error messages, push notification text, notification e-mails (in the recipient's language). Password reset e-mails are sent in English.
  • Not translated by Evey: media metadata (titles, plot summaries, genres) comes from your metadata provider (TMDB/OMDb) in the Metadata language set in the setup wizard or in Admin → Server Config → Language & Region (EVEY_METADATA_LANGUAGE is only the default), which is independent of the UI language. Your own libraries, file names, and anything you type are stored as-is.

So the UI can be in French while a movie's synopsis is in English (or vice versa) - they're two separate settings.

docs.title: Supported UI languages
docs.text: Six: English (en), French (fr), German (de), Spanish (es), Chinese (zh), Hindi (hi). English is the source language and the fallback: any string missing in another language falls back to English rather than showing a blank or a key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One source of truth: /i18n/<locale>/*.yaml at the repo root, split into namespaces (common, auth, media, player, admin, errors, notifications, mobile, downloads, requests). The same catalog drives every surface.
  • The server loads it and serves it at GET /api/v1/i18n/{locale}, and uses it directly for translated API error messages and notification text.
  • The web, mobile, and TV apps load translations from that endpoint (i18next + http-backend), cache them locally, and keep <html lang> in sync with the active language so assistive tech announces the right language.
  • Language is picked from your account preference, falling back to the browser/device language (Accept-Language is parsed, region stripped: fr-FR → fr), then to the Server language of Admin → Server Config → Language & Region (which also sets the language of new accounts), then to English.
  • Interpolation and pluralization use i18next ({{count}} etc.).

docs.title: Honest limitations
docs.text:
• Completeness varies. English is authoritative and always complete; the other five are kept at parity by hand with a check script, but a brand-new feature may land in English first and fall back until translated.
  • No right-to-left languages yet. There's no Arabic/Hebrew/Persian, and the layout has not been built or tested for RTL - adding one is real work (CSS logical properties, dir handling), not just a translation file.
  • Translations aren't professionally reviewed. They're community/maintainer quality. Corrections are welcome.
  • Locale-aware formatting is partial. Dates/numbers rely on the platform Intl/browser locale and aren't uniformly wired on every screen.

docs.title: Adding or fixing a language
docs.text:
1. Copy i18n/en/ to i18n/<your-locale>/ and translate the YAML values (keep the keys).
  2. Add the locale to the allowlist in internal/pkg/i18n/i18n.go (supportedLocales).
  3. Keep the key set identical across locales - the parity check fails otherwise.

docs.title: Where this stands
docs.text: Evey is built with semantic HTML, ARIA labels, and React Native accessibility props, and a few things below are deliberate. But it has not been formally audited against WCAG, there is no automated accessibility testing in the suite, and it has not been systematically tested with screen readers. Parts of it are likely usable with assistive tech; parts are likely not. If you depend on AT, expect rough edges and please report specifics.

docs.title: What's in place
docs.text:
• Reduced motion: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is honored globally - animations and transitions are effectively disabled when your OS asks for it.
  • Language for AT: <html lang> tracks the active UI language.
  • Keyboard (player): full keyboard controls with an on-screen shortcuts overlay (?), and shortcuts are suppressed while you're typing in a field.
  • Labelled controls: icon-only buttons and sliders carry aria-label on web and accessibilityLabel/accessibilityRole on mobile (the larger share of interactive controls, not all).
  • Theming: five themes ship in-box (default dark, AMOLED, dark-red, light-default, light-blue); more via theme plugins.
  • Android TV: D-pad focus handling for remote navigation.

docs.title: Honest gaps (not done yet)
docs.text:
• No screen-reader pass. NVDA/VoiceOver/TalkBack flows are unverified; some custom widgets (menus, modals, the seek bar, track pickers) may not announce their state or role correctly.
  • Focus management isn't audited. Focus-visible styling and focus order in dialogs/overlays are inconsistent in places.
  • Contrast is measured for the built-in themes only. A unit test (frontend/packages/theme/src/contrast.test.ts) holds every shipped theme to WCAG AA 4.5:1 for the accent, the three text ramps and the danger set against the background and both surfaces; the TV app re-checks its derived tokens. Theme plugins and the colours a plugin injects at runtime are not checked - a custom theme can still fail in spots. AAA is not targeted.
  • No in-app text scaling beyond browser/OS zoom, and no dedicated high-contrast mode.
  • Subtitle styling on mobile is limited (a constraint of the underlying expo-video player), though subtitle/caption tracks themselves play.

docs.title: Reporting an issue
docs.text: Tell us the page/screen, the specific control, what you expected, and the assistive tech + version you used. Concrete reports get fixed; "it's not accessible" can't be acted on. a11y fixes are handled best-effort.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Evey runs as one container. The image serves the API and the web interface on one port, and runs its own database (Postgres) and search engine (Meilisearch) inside it, with their passwords generated on the first start. The compose file below is the whole installation: no .env, no privileged mode, no memory or CPU setting.

Not the repository's docker-compose.yml

The docker-compose.yml at the root of the Git repository is a different layout (Postgres as a separate service, a bundled Caddy, a required .env). Use the file on this page. The other layout is described in Advanced deployments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker with Compose v2 (docker compose, not the older docker-compose).
  • A persistent disk for Evey's data (the compose file below keeps it in ./evey-data, next to the file).
  • An x86-64 host, or ARM64 with a release tag: see ARM hosts.

Evey serves plain HTTP. To reach it from outside your home over HTTPS, put a reverse proxy in front of it later: see Remote access and HTTPS.

docs.title: The compose file
docs.text:
Save this as docker-compose.yml and replace the media path on the last volume line.

docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    image: eveyproject/evey:beta-0.0.1 # (1)!
    container_name: evey-server
    ports:
      - "9091:9091" # (2)!
    volumes:
      - ./evey-data:/data # (3)!
      - evey-cache:/cache # (4)!
      - /path/to/your/media:/media # (5)!
    stop_grace_period: 60s # (6)!
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  evey-cache:
  1. Evey is in beta and has no numbered release yet, so there is no latest tag: beta-0.0.1 follows the development branch and moves with every change. To run the same code from one pull to the next, put an immutable sha-<commit> tag here instead: see Backups and updates.
  2. The API and the web interface, on one port, in plain HTTP.
  3. Everything Evey owns: database, signing key, generated passwords, search index, timeline thumbnails, artwork, logs, backups, plugins. This is the folder to back up.
  4. Transcoding cache: segments, resized photos and covers. It can be deleted at any time and refills on demand.
  5. Your media. Mounted read-write on purpose: the repairs of Media health rewrite files in place. Append :ro for a read-only library and those repairs will fail. More folders are mounted as /media2, /media3...
  6. Leaves the embedded database time to stop cleanly on docker stop. Docker's default of 10 seconds is short for a large catalogue.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f evey

On the first start the server generates its signing key and passwords in ./evey-data, creates the database and applies its migrations. Nothing has to be prepared by hand.

Then open http://<server-address>:9091. A server with no administrator opens on the setup wizard: continue with First setup.

docs.title: Where the data lives
docs.text: Location Contains Can be deleted? ./evey-data Database, signing key, generated passwords, search index, timeline thumbnails, artwork, logs, backups, plugins No. Losing it loses every account, watch history and setting. Only meili/ inside it can go: the search index is rebuilt from the database with evey admin reindex-search. evey-cache volume Transcoded segments, resized photos and covers Yes. Regenerated on demand. Your media folders Your files Evey does not delete them; removing a title in Evey removes it from the library, not from the disk. It writes there in three cases: a repair run from Media health (the original is kept as a backup), subtitles downloaded from OpenSubtitles (a .subtitles folder next to the film), and a probe file of a few seconds that checks the folder watcher still receives events.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Each of these is a few lines added to the same file.

A second media folder. Add - /other/path:/media2 under volumes:.

File ownership. By default the container adopts the owner of your /media mount, so that repairs can write. To choose it yourself, set PUID and PGID under environment: (the output of id -u and id -g). The container starts as root only to apply that mapping; the server itself never runs as root.

A graphics card for transcoding. Map the device into the container: see Hardware acceleration.

Behind a reverse proxy you already run. See Remote access and HTTPS.

On a NAS (Synology Container Manager, QNAP Container Station)
  • Create the evey-data folder before the first start. These interfaces refuse a bind mount whose folder does not exist, unlike the Docker command line. Nothing else needs creating.
  • Set PUID and PGID to the NAS user that owns the media (id <user> over SSH; on Synology typically around 1026, group 100). A NAS share is often owned by root, which the automatic detection never adopts.
  • Intel NAS with Quick Sync: add the devices: and group_add: lines described in Hardware acceleration.

docs.title: What you do not need to configure
docs.text: Transcoding capacity, the graphics card, the playback method for each device and remote access are decided by the server: it measures the machine on its first quiet moment, detects the hardware you mapped, and opens remote access when you give it a public address. Settings that can change later (server name, schedules, limits, API keys) are in the admin panel, not in the compose file. The environment variables that do exist are listed in the Configuration reference.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Evey tells each profile when new films, series, seasons, episodes or albums arrive. Administrators also hear about failed backups, plugin errors and new media requests, and whoever made a request hears back when it is answered.

docs.title: Where notifications appear
docs.text:
• In every app: the bell, with an unread count. Always on, nothing to set up. A notification is kept 30 days. The list only shows titles from libraries the account can open.
  • Browser push: on the web, each profile turns on Push Notifications in Settings → Notifications, once per browser. The server creates its push keys on first start; see E-mail and notifications to bring your own. Browsers allow push only on an HTTPS address (or localhost); elsewhere the setting says Push notifications need an HTTPS address: open this server over HTTPS to turn them on. The Android and TV apps do not receive push notifications.
  • E-mail: once e-mail is set up, every notification is also sent to the account's address, in the profile's language, with a link to the server. An account with several profiles receives one e-mail per event. There is no per-user opt-out.

docs.title: Setting up e-mail
docs.text:
Admin → Server Config → Email / SMTP: the mail server, its port, the account to sign in with, the sender address and the TLS mode. Saving applies at once, without a restart. Send test email sends a short message to your own account's address with the saved settings, and shows the mail server's answer when it fails.

starttls upgrades a plain connection (usually port 587), ssl uses TLS from the start (usually port 465), none sends without encryption.

The EVEY_SMTP_* variables are the fallback, used while the card has no host:

.env
EVEY_SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
EVEY_SMTP_PORT=587
EVEY_SMTP_USERNAME=notifications@example.com
EVEY_SMTP_PASSWORD=your-smtp-password
EVEY_SMTP_FROM=noreply@example.com
EVEY_SMTP_TLS=starttls

As soon as a host is saved in the card, every field comes from the card and the variables are ignored, so the server never sends the variables' credentials to a mail server typed in the panel.

E-mail is used for notifications and password resets; invitations are links you share yourself.

docs.title: What each profile receives
docs.text:
In Settings → Notifications, each profile picks a level for Movies, Series and Music:

Level New titles notified All Every one. The default. Relevant Only those sharing a genre with the profile's usual genres. Important only Currently the same as Relevant. Disabled None.

A genre counts as usual when it appears in at least 3 of the profile's last 200 playbacks. A title without genres is never notified at the Relevant and Important only levels.

Several episodes of one series arriving within 24 hours make a single notification that counts them, and none is sent when the series or the season was just announced.

docs.title: Password recovery
docs.text:
1. Set up e-mail (see above).
  2. Turn on Password recovery in Admin → Server Config → Server Settings. It applies immediately.
  3. The sign-in page then shows Forgot your password?, which e-mails a reset link.

Without SMTP the link stays hidden, even with the option on.

docs.title: OIDC / SSO Setup
docs.text: Evey supports Single Sign-On via OpenID Connect: Keycloak, Authentik, Authelia, Google or any other OIDC provider. The sign-in page of the web and Android apps then shows Sign in with SSO next to the password form.

docs.title: 1. Register Evey with the provider
docs.text:
Create a client (or application) in the provider with the Authorization Code grant, the scopes openid email profile, a client secret, and the two addresses the Single sign-on (SSO) card shows under Register these addresses at your provider:

Field Value Redirect URI https://<your address>/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback Post-logout redirect URI https://<your address>/login

Both are built from the server's public address (Admin → Remote Access): set that first if people reach Evey under another address.

docs.title: 2. Configure Evey
docs.text:
Admin → Server Config → Single sign-on (SSO):

Field Effect Enable single sign-on Shows the SSO button on the sign-in screens. Issuer URL The provider's address, without /.well-known/openid-configuration. Client ID, Client secret The client registered above. The secret is kept on the server and never shown again; leaving the dots keeps it. Allowed e-mail domains Comma separated.
