When set, only these addresses are accepted, and the provider must confirm the address. Button label Optional, replaces "Sign in with SSO". Link to existing accounts by verified e-mail On by default. See below. Create accounts for new SSO users Off unless e-mail domains are allowed. See below. Library access for new SSO accounts All libraries, or Only the selected libraries.

Test connection checks that the issuer answers. Save SSO settings applies at once, without a restart. The Status line says whether the provider is reachable, with the last error if it is not.

The EVEY_OIDC_* variables of Accounts and sign-in are the fallback: the card says when its values come from them, and saving the card takes over.

The server never waits for the provider: it starts even when the provider is down, the SSO button stays hidden while the provider cannot be reached, and password sign-in keeps working. The provider is contacted again on the next sign-in attempt, at most every 30 seconds.

docs.title: Who can sign in
docs.text:
1. An account already signed in with this provider before signs in again, unless it is disabled.
  2. Otherwise, with Link to existing accounts by verified e-mail on, an existing account with the same e-mail is linked to the provider and signed in, but only when the provider confirms the address. The account keeps its password. Administrator accounts are never linked this way.
  3. Otherwise, with Create accounts for new SSO users on, a new account is created, with one profile and the library access chosen in the card. Its username is the provider's preferred_username, otherwise the part of the e-mail before @; a name already taken gets a short suffix.

Create accounts for new SSO users is off by default when no e-mail domain is allowed: with a public provider such as Google, anyone holding an account there could otherwise get one on your server. When it is off, only existing accounts can sign in with SSO.

When a sign-in is refused, the sign-in page says why: the e-mail domain is not allowed, no account matches and sign-up is off, the account is disabled, the account exists but could not be linked, or the provider is unavailable.

docs.title: Signing out
docs.text: When the provider publishes a logout endpoint, signing out of Evey after an SSO sign-in also ends the session at the provider, then returns to the Evey sign-in page. The card says whether the provider supports it.

docs.title: Serving a video - the HLS playback path
docs.text:
This is the read path: what happens when a player asks for a video, from the first master.m3u8 request down to the bytes of a segment. It is the counterpart to the scan pipeline in ARCHITECTURE.md (the write path that primes the read model), and the deep-dive behind CODEBASE_MAP.md "Golden path 4".

The playback path is VITAL and spread across ~8 files in the http adapter. There is no single function that runs the whole flow - this document is the map.

docs.title: The mental model: 3 questions, 2 engines, 1 key
docs.text:
Serving a video reduces to answering three questions, then packaging the answer, with everything addressed by one hash:

  • Q1 - Can I read the file cheaply? Probe dispatch, by file extension: .mkv/.webm and .mp4/.mov go to mkvgo (head-only, no process); everything else, and any fast-path failure, goes to ffprobe (the authority).
  • Q2 - Can the client play it as-is? The playback decision, taken per track: video copy vs transcode, audio copy vs transcode vs the wasm AC-3 path. Video and audio are decided independently - the common case is "copy the video, re-encode the audio to AAC".
  • Q3 - How much can this host encode? The calibrated capability (from the measurement taken at the first quiet moment) plus admission (which ladder rung fits, is there a slot).

Two engines run through all of it:

  • mkvgo - reads and repackages (remux / on-demand) without spawning a process. Free.
  • ffmpeg / ffprobe - decodes, re-encodes, probes by spawning a process. Costly.

One key: everything (cache directory, ffmpeg session, segment URLs) is addressed by the decision fingerprint - a hash of the decision. Same bytes ⇒ same hash ⇒ one shared encode. The whole system's correctness rests on that hash being stable between the manifest a player holds and every segment it later fetches.

docs.title: Reading order - follow one request through the code
docs.text:
Open these in sequence to trace a single playback request end to end:

  1. Entry · internal/adapters/driving/http/transcode_handler_vod.go - serveHTTP authenticates, then dispatches to master / variant / segment / audio.
  2. The plan · http/transcode_vod_plan.go marshals the request into a PlaybackRequest; app/transcoding/playback_plan_resolver.go - PlanResolver.Resolve returns one immutable PlaybackPlan: the decision (Q2), the ladder class, the shaped ladder, the hardware route, the packager and the fingerprint. Every manifest and segment of the session is served from it (ADR-0030). makeDecision and buildFingerprint in http/transcode_vod_fingerprint.go are thin wrappers for the call sites without a plan (prewarm, on-demand master).
  3. Q2 · Decision · internal/app/transcoding/decision.go - MakePlaybackDecisionWithPrefs (pure): the per-track copy/transcode brain. The resolver layers on the request-time pins (vd= / ad=), the audio-resync override, etc.
  4. Q3 · Capability · internal/app/transcoding/calibration_service.go - Current() returns domain/transcoding.Derive(report, policy) (derive.go): the host's ceilings, derived from the last calibration.
  5. Ladder and admission · the resolver shapes the ladder (complexity class → producer profiles → source/capability caps → CMCD/AV1 caps → admission route and ceiling), then freezes it on the admission pin (admission_shaper.go, FreezeLadder), read verbatim on every later call - the cache-hash invariant made structural. video_session_limiter.go holds the capacity slot; the route spills from hardware to software when full.
  6. Fingerprint · a DecisionFingerprint (type + Hash() in app/transcoding/segment_cache.go), assembled by the resolver. The hash is the cache key.
  7. Producing the bytes · copy → mkvgo app/transcoding/ondemand.go (port) / adapters/driven/mkvgo/ondemand.go; transcode → ffmpeg adapters/driven/ffmpeg/hls_transcoder.go (BuildFFmpegArgs is pure; segments land in /cache/transcode/segments/<hash>/).
  8. Packaging · app/transcoding/manifest_generator.go - master.m3u8 / stream_N.m3u8; manifest_generator_dash.go - manifest.mpd.

docs.title: The two engines, by cost
docs.text:
The probe dispatcher (adapters/driven/prober/dispatcher.go) is a chain-of-responsibility keyed on extension: it tries mkvgo, and falls back to ffprobe on any doubt (parse error, panic, unmappable result, a dropped MP4 media track, DoVi profile 5, unreadable colour). Both fast-paths are always on (nil gates in wire.go); ffprobe is the safety net, never bypassed. A second, identical dispatcher (keyframe_dispatcher.go) handles the seek index.

Operation mkvgo (free) ffprobe / ffmpeg (costly) Metadata probe (codec, dims, HDR, bitrate, duration) .mkv/.webm/.mp4/.mov head-only everything else, or fallback Frame-rate mode (cfr/vfr) AnalyzeFrameRateMode - (migrated) Remux MKV→MP4 (no re-encode) RemuxToMP4 - On-demand HLS/DASH (copy rung) OnDemandPackager - Video re-encode / HDR tonemap - hls_transcoder.go Interlace detect (idet), seek-landing, chromaprint, DoVi P5 - (needs decode / side-data) ffmpeg / ffprobe

Three ffprobe forks still run on MKV/MP4 sources whose data mkvgo already exposes (duration in trickplay.go, bitrate+dims in complexity_classifier.go, playback audio-delay in audio_delay.go) - candidates to migrate; small CPU win, mostly wiring.

docs.title: Audio is decided separately from video
docs.text: makeDecision produces VideoDecision and AudioDecision independently. The "copy rung" (isCopyRequest) is gated on the video only; even a copied video usually carries a re-encoded AAC track alongside. The audio decision has three outcomes: copy, transcode to AAC (ffmpeg, light), or - for AC-3 / E-AC-3 on a browser that can't decode it natively - the wasm path: the master is made video-only with an #EVEY-AUDIO-URI tag, the AC-3 is copied (mkvgo od_audio if the plan builds, else ffmpeg -c:a copy), and ac3go.wasm decodes it to PCM in the browser (WasmAudioEngine.ts), clock-locked to the video. Safari is excluded by capability, not by name: canWasmDecodeAC3() returns true only when the browser reports it cannot play AC-3 natively - Safari reports it can.

docs.title: Packaging: CMAF, HLS, DASH
docs.text:
The container is always CMAF (fMP4): a per-variant init.mp4 plus .m4s segments. (The MPEG-TS branch in hls_transcoder.go is dead - needsFMP4Segments always returns true.) Over the same segments:

  • HLS (master.m3u8 → stream_N.m3u8 → EXT-X-MAP init + .m4s) - both engines.
  • DASH (manifest.mpd) - on the mkvgo copy path the packager's own manifest (OnDemandPlan.HasDASH, byte-identical, zero storage, disabled under AES-128); on the ffmpeg path a manifest declared from the plan over the same fragments the HLS playlists address (ManifestGenerator.MPD), written before any fragment exists. What makes it honest is the segment grid (domain/transcoding.SegmentGrid): every transcoded rung is cut on the same whole number of frames (72 at 23.976 fps, 75 at 25, 90 at 29.97), so a segment is exact in the video track's ticks and identical across the switch set; the copy fallback declares its keyframe plan. A source whose frame rate is unknown or variable stays on the legacy 3 s clock, keeps HLS, and answers 404 on manifest.mpd. No client is switched to DASH: HLS stays the default everywhere. mkvgo's DASHFromCMAF over the produced fragments is the parity oracle (internal/pkg/cmafparity, TestDASHGridIntegration at 23.976/25/29.97 fps: cold, seek, two-rung switch set, separate audio within one AAC frame).

Per-session URLs are re-baked (transcode_vod_manifest_rebake.go) to carry the stream token, for HLS and DASH alike, including cookie-less Chromecast.

docs.title: Design patterns in play
docs.text:
• Ports & adapters (hexagonal) - the app layer talks to interfaces (StreamProber, BenchmarkRunner, OnDemandPackager, StreamProducer); ffmpeg and mkvgo implement them. A new engine is a new adapter.
  • Strategy - StreamProducer (software / hardware / copy), picked by a ProducerSelector.
  • Chain of responsibility with fallback - the probe/keyframe dispatchers (mkvgo → ffprobe authority).
  • Content-addressed cache - the DecisionFingerprint hash keys the cache and the ffmpeg session.
  • Pure core / imperative shell - Derive, MakePlaybackDecision, the cost model are pure and unit-tested without ffmpeg or a DB.
  • Immutable value object - StreamPlan: the admission decision, emitted once, never mutated, so the URLs↔bytes invariant holds by construction.
  • Graceful degradation - a safe fallback at every step: 720p default capability, hw→software spill, copy→transcode, mkvgo→ffprobe.

docs.title: The decision brain: the app-layer PlanResolver
docs.text: The request-handling brain - decision pins, ladder shaping, hardware routing, fingerprint assembly, copy-rung routing, producer pick - lives in the app layer: PlanResolver (app/transcoding/playback_plan_resolver.go), the concrete PlaybackPlanResolver (playback_plan.go). Each request is resolved once: the http adapter marshals the *http.Request into a transport-free PlaybackRequest (http/transcode_vod_plan.go) and serves off the returned immutable PlaybackPlan. Every consumer - manifest input, shed probe, stale-URL seal, producer pick, segment key - reads that single resolution, so within a request the cache-hash invariant holds by construction (and the segment hot path went from ~5 profile prefs fetches to 1). The source-fact helpers (codec, HDR, SAR, ten-bit…) live alongside in app/transcoding/source_facts.go; the adapter keeps thin aliases. Across requests the invariant still rests on URL baking: every input to the decision must be baked into the child URLs, or a mid-play poll can flip the plan under the player (querySuffix in manifest_generator.go).

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Plugins add to Evey what it does not do by itself: metadata sources, notification channels, webhook receivers, home-page sections, player overlays, and themes. Each plugin is a separate process that talks to the server through a local socket, confined by a sandbox and limited to the permissions its manifest declares. Its interface, if it has one, runs in an isolated frame of the page.

Without plugins. With the example weather plugin: a section at the top, drawn in its own frame.

docs.title: Installing and managing plugins
docs.text:
Admin → Plugins installs a plugin from its ZIP file. Before anything is installed, the preview shows:

Admin → Plugins: the runtimes available, the resource limits, and one card per plugin.
  • the permissions the plugin declares, the slots of the interface it wants to appear in, and the hosts it will contact;
  • what the static analysis found in its code;
  • its signature, when the server checks signatures.

A plugin whose analysis finds a critical pattern is refused. An update of an installed plugin goes through the same preview; when it asks for new permissions, slots or hosts, you must accept the difference explicitly.

Signed plugins

A plugin author can sign the ZIP with cosign, and you decide what an unsigned or badly signed plugin does. To verify signatures, give the server the author's public key and pick a policy:

EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY=/etc/evey/cosign.pub
EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY=warn      # off | warn (default) | enforce

Then pick the ZIP and its .zip.sig file in Admin → Plugins. With warn, a failure is shown in the preview and the Security Dashboard; with enforce, the install or update is refused. Nothing is verified without a public key, and the server needs no cosign binary. Authors: see Sign your plugin.

Each plugin then has, on its card: enable or disable, update, logs, and its resource limits (memory, processes, disk, CPU priority). The Host sandbox line of the Security Dashboard shows the sandbox mode actually in force on this host: see Plugin sandbox setup if it shows basic.

Plugins are enabled by default. EVEY_PLUGINS_ENABLED=false turns the subsystem off entirely.

docs.title: What a plugin can and cannot do
docs.text:
A plugin sees its own directory and not the server's data, has no direct network access (a plugin allowed on the network reaches only the hosts it declared, through the server), and cannot start processes unless it declares the subprocess permission. The permissions a plugin can ask for are listed in Permissions and slots. How the sandbox works, and what it still cannot prevent, is described in Security model and plugin sandbox.

Review a third-party plugin before installing it, as you would any software: once a host is on a plugin's list, the server cannot inspect what the plugin sends to it.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph server["Evey server"]
    host["HostService<br/>checks every call against<br/>the declared permissions"]
    ui["Web interface<br/>plugin slots"]
  end
  subgraph plugin["Plugin, in its sandbox"]
    backend["PluginService<br/>your backend process"]
    front["Frontend module<br/>isolated iframe"]
  end
  backend <-->|"gRPC over a Unix socket"| host
  front <-->|"postMessage bridge"| ui
  host -->|"Fetch: declared hosts only"| net(("Internet"))

A plugin can be written in any language its entrypoint can launch. Generated gRPC stubs ship for Python, Node.js, PHP, Ruby, Dart, Java and Swift; Go stubs are generated with protoc-gen-go; compiled binaries need the native-binary permission.

Page Contents Writing a plugin Prerequisites, first plugin, the install loop, signing, distribution. Start here. Plugin API reference The manifest, the backend calls and data store, the evey.* frontend bridge, capabilities. Permissions and slots What a manifest may declare, what is checked at install, the external fetch rules, the slots. Themes Restyling the interface with CSS and a sandboxed script. Webhooks and API keys Integrating Evey with other tools without writing a plugin.

docs.title: Privacy policy
docs.text:
Last updated: 2026-10-04.

This policy covers the Evey apps for Android and Android TV. The Evey project runs no service that receives your data: no account with us, no analytics, no advertising, no crash reporting to us. The apps talk to the Evey server that you, or the person who invited you, installed and runs.

docs.title: What the apps send, and to whom
docs.text:
To your Evey server, and to nothing else we operate. The apps send what a media player needs to work:

  • your username and password when you sign in (or the Quick Connect code), then a session token;
  • what you browse, search, play, rate, favourite or request, and your playback position, so you can resume on another device;
  • the name of the device (as Android reports it), so you can tell your devices apart in Play On and in the server's list of sessions;
  • technical playback reports: which audio and video formats the device can decode, and errors met while playing, so the server can pick a stream the device can play;
  • a picture, only when you choose one as a profile avatar, and files you pick yourself (an external subtitle, a plugin, a backup) as an administrator.

Who can read this data is up to the operator of that server. The Evey project has no access to it.

To third parties, only in these cases:

  • Posters and album art. Some pictures shown in media requests and music come straight from their public source (The Movie Database, the Cover Art Archive, IMDb). The device fetches them like a web browser would, which reveals its IP address to that host.
  • Casting. Casting to a Chromecast goes through Google Cast, part of Google Play services on your phone. The Chromecast loads the Evey receiver page from cast.eveyproject.org, hosted by GitHub Pages. The media itself streams from your server.
  • Voice search on Android TV. The microphone button hands over to the television's own voice recognizer (usually Google's). The app receives the recognized text, never the recording.
  • Links you open. A trailer, a The Movie Database or IMDb page, or the Play Store page for an update opens in the matching app or browser, under that service's own policy.
  • Plugins. Plugins are installed by the server's administrator. A plugin may show content from an outside service (a weather plugin, for instance).

docs.title: What stays on the device
docs.text: The server address, your session token (in Android's encrypted storage), your preferences, and the films and music you download for offline viewing. Removing the app removes them. Biometric unlock (fingerprint or face), when you turn it on, is handled by Android: the app only learns whether it succeeded.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permission Why Internet, Wi-Fi state Reach your server, tell your home network apart from the outside. Camera Scan a Quick Connect QR code. Nothing is recorded or sent. Notifications, foreground service Show playback and download progress, keep playing with the screen off. Biometrics Optional app lock.

The phone app does not have the microphone permission.

docs.title: This website
docs.text: eveyproject.org is hosted by GitHub Pages, which sees the visitor's IP address. The site serves its own fonts and scripts, so the browser contacts no other service. It sets no cookie of its own and has no analytics.

docs.title: Children
docs.text: The apps are not aimed at children. Kids profiles are set up by the server's operator, who holds that data.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Questions about this policy: contact@eveyproject.org. For data held on an Evey server, contact the person who runs that server.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
Evey serves both the API and the web UI on port 9091 (plain HTTP). A reverse proxy only needs to terminate TLS and forward everything to evey:9091: there is no separate frontend to build or serve.

Wherever you run a proxy, tell Evey its public URL and which proxy to trust. The simplest place is Admin → Remote Access: an https:// External URL and, when the proxy is a container, its network in Trusted proxies. Both apply without a restart. The same answers can come from the environment, for an installation described entirely as code (the panel wins when both are set):

.env
EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL=https://media.example.com
EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=172.16.0.0/12       # only needed if the proxy is a container; loopback is always trusted

An https:// address is what tells Evey a proxy terminates TLS in front of it: cookies get the Secure flag, HSTS is sent, and X-Forwarded-Proto from a trusted proxy is honoured. No separate switch is needed (the former EVEY_FORWARDED_PROTO is still accepted as an override, but deprecated).

docs.title: Streaming - what a proxy's defaults do to it
docs.text:
Evey works behind a reverse proxy left on its defaults: every long-lived response either sends bytes continuously (HLS segments, direct play, transcode output) or pings the client every 30 s (the event streams), so a default read timeout never fires. Two things are still worth knowing:

  • Buffering. A proxy that buffers responses (nginx does by default) reads a direct-play file into its own buffers and temp files before the client gets it - functional, but a multi-GB film then transits through the proxy host's disk. proxy_buffering off on the streaming paths avoids that.
  • Scans. /api/v1/libraries/*/scan streams progress for as long as the scan runs; a proxy that caps a response's total duration (rare - nginx and Caddy do not by default) would cut it short. The scan itself continues server-side regardless.

The paths concerned:

/api/v1/media/*/hls/*
/api/v1/media/*/stream
/api/v1/libraries/*/scan

The bundled Caddy and the Nginx/Traefik examples below set both (no buffering, no timeout) on these paths. With a UI-driven proxy such as Nginx Proxy Manager, the defaults are fine and the tuning is an optional snippet.

docs.title: Security headers & CSP - read this if your proxy sets its own
docs.text:
Evey emits a complete Content-Security-Policy. If your proxy passes it through, you're done.

Many setups instead strip it (header_down -Content-Security-Policy in Caddy) and curate their own - that's fine, but then your policy must keep these tokens or features break silently:

Token Directive Breaks without it 'self' frame-src Every plugin UI and theme script (blank iframe). They run in /plugin-frame.html, a page of Evey framed by the app (see below). 'wasm-unsafe-eval' script-src Browser AC-3/E-AC-3 playback (the ac3go WebAssembly decoder can't compile → the film plays muted). This is the narrow token that permits Wasm compilation only - NOT general eval(). https://www.gstatic.com script-src (+ frame-src) The Google Cast sender SDK never loads → no cast button for anyone. It is the only way a browser can discover Chromecasts on the user's own LAN. blob: media-src MSE playback (hls.js attaches the stream via a blob URL). blob: worker-src hls.js silently falls back to main-thread demuxing (choppier on mobile).

A known-good policy for a curating proxy:

default-src 'self'; base-uri 'self'; object-src 'none';
img-src 'self' https: data: blob:; media-src 'self' blob:;
style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' https://www.gstatic.com;
connect-src 'self' https: wss:; worker-src 'self' blob:; font-src 'self' data:;
frame-src 'self' https://www.gstatic.com

base-uri and object-src have no fallback to default-src, so a policy that omits them leaves <base href> injection and <object>/<embed> embedding unrestricted. Keep them if you curate your own policy.

script-src has no 'unsafe-inline': a script injected into the page does not run. Do not add it back - nothing in the app needs it.

Two pages carry their own policy, sent by the app; leave the app's header on those two paths:

  • /plugin-frame.html, the page plugin UIs and theme scripts run in. Its policy sandboxes it (even opened outside an iframe), limits its network to the hosts the plugin's manifest declares, and lets only the app frame it, so it also sends X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN: do not overwrite that with DENY on this path, or every plugin UI stays blank.
  • /cast-receiver.html, described below.

One page needs a wider policy: /cast-receiver.html, the page a Chromecast loads when it plays from Evey. The Cast player injects styles, fonts and images from www.gstatic.com into it, and the app sends that page its own policy for this reason. Leave the app's header on that path, or apply this policy to that path only:

default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' https://www.gstatic.com; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://www.gstatic.com; img-src 'self' data: https: blob:; media-src 'self' blob: https:; worker-src 'self' blob:; font-src 'self' data: https://www.gstatic.com; connect-src 'self' https: wss:; frame-src https://www.gstatic.com; base-uri 'self'; object-src 'none'

Rules of thumb:

  • Exactly one CSP header must reach the browser. With two (e.g. the app's AND your proxy's, or Caddy's AND Nginx Proxy Manager's "Advanced" snippet), browsers enforce the intersection - the strictest wins and the failure is silent. Check with curl -sI https://your.domain | grep -ci content-security-policy → must print 1.
  • Keep the policy on ONE line. A CSP split across lines in a proxy config is a classic silent corruption: the join swallows the characters at the seam (...gstatic.com; connect-src became ...gstaticonnect-src once, which disabled the Cast SDK and merged two directives).
  • Check the plugin frame keeps its own policy: curl -sI https://your.domain/plugin-frame.html | grep -i -e content-security -e x-frame must show sandbox allow-scripts and SAMEORIGIN.

Every bundled example reads the domain from one place: EVEY_DOMAIN in your .env. Set it once; Caddy, Nginx and Traefik all pick it up.

.env
EVEY_DOMAIN=media.example.com

docs.title: Caddy (bundled)
docs.text: The repo ships docker/Caddyfile (built into an image by docker/Dockerfile.caddy): it gets automatic HTTPS for EVEY_DOMAIN and proxies everything to evey:9091, with the streaming exceptions already set. It also curates the canonical security headers/CSP from the section above (and strips the app's own CSP so exactly one reaches the browser). Add a caddy service to your compose (see the caddy service in the repo docker-compose.yml).

docs.title: Behind a proxy you already run (TLS terminated upstream)
docs.text:
On a NAS that already has a reverse proxy (the vendor's, Nginx Proxy Manager, a Traefik on a shared Docker network), no Caddy is needed: Evey emits its own security headers and a complete CSP, and the streaming rules can only be enforced by the proxy that faces the client anyway - a second proxy behind it adds nothing. Put the evey service on that proxy's network and target evey-server:9091 (the container name; the service name evey resolves too):

docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    # no ports: the proxy is the only way in
    environment:
      EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL: https://media.example.com
      EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES: 172.16.0.0/12     # narrow to the proxy's subnet once known
    # ...
networks:
  default:
    name: proxy-net
    external: true

Then, in that proxy, for the route to evey-server:9091: forward X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto, enable WebSocket support, and apply the streaming rules above (no buffering, no read/write timeout on the streaming paths) - the Nginx, Traefik and Nginx Proxy Manager sections below show the exact lines.

docs.title: Nginx
docs.text: Use examples/nginx/evey.conf.template (a ready compose is at examples/nginx/docker-compose.nginx.yml). The nginx image renders it at startup with EVEY_DOMAIN substituted - certificates must exist under the matching file names. It proxies to evey:9091 with streaming buffering disabled - no frontend build step.

docs.title: Traefik
docs.text:
See examples/traefik/docker-compose.traefik.yml:

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f examples/traefik/docker-compose.traefik.yml up -d

docs.title: Nginx Proxy Manager
docs.text:
The evey container must be on the network NPM uses (see "Behind a proxy you already run" above). Then, Edit Proxy Host:

  1. Details: Scheme http, Forward Hostname evey-server, Forward Port 9091. Websockets Support: on (SyncPlay). Cache Assets: off - it would cache media segments and playlists with a fixed expiry. Block Common Exploits can stay on (turn it off if a search or a plugin upload ever answers 403 for no reason).
  2. SSL: your certificate, Force SSL, HTTP/2. HSTS is optional here - the app already sends it. That is all: NPM forwards X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto and the Host header on its own, and its default timeouts never fire on Evey's streams (see the streaming section above).

Optional - keep NPM from buffering direct-play files through its own disk: Advanced → Custom Nginx Configuration (the Custom Locations tab cannot express the regex):

# Plugin uploads (up to 100 MB) and backup restores (up to 2 GB).
client_max_body_size 2G;

# Streaming - no buffering, no timeout.
location ~ ^/api/v1/media/.+/(hls|stream) {
    proxy_pass http://evey-server:9091;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_request_buffering off;
    proxy_read_timeout 0;
    proxy_send_timeout 0;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}

# Library scans stream their progress for as long as the scan runs.
location ~ ^/api/v1/libraries/.+/scan {
    proxy_pass http://evey-server:9091;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_read_timeout 0;
    proxy_send_timeout 0;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}

Every other path (the web UI, the rest of the API, the SyncPlay WebSocket) goes through NPM's own proxy block, which the Details tab configures. Skip the snippet and nothing breaks - it only changes where big files are buffered.

docs.title: Real client IPs and the remote-access gate
docs.text:
Once your proxy forwards the real client address, Evey can tell a viewer at home from one on the internet. That is what the WAN bitrate cap and the remote-access gate act on, so the two settings only behave correctly together:

  • The trusted proxies (panel or EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES) must cover the proxy (172.16.0.0/12 when it is a container on the Docker network; nothing to add when it runs on the host, loopback is always trusted). Whatever you set is ADDED to the loopback baseline - it never replaces it, so a Docker value cannot silently stop the gate from seeing real client addresses.
  • Chained proxies each need to preserve X-Forwarded-For. In Caddy that is servers { trusted_proxies static private_ranges }; nginx uses proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;.

Turning this on changes who counts as remote. Before it, every request looked like it came from the proxy's own private address, so everyone was classified LAN. After it, real remote clients are correctly identified - and if remote access is disabled they are refused on every route (403 {"code":"remote_access_disabled"}), although no application setting changed.

Evey guards against it: remote access defaults to enabled whenever a public URL is configured and no explicit choice was made, the state is logged at every boot, refusals are logged with the client IP, evey admin doctor fails loudly on "published but refusing", and the admin panel shows a warning. If you change proxy trust settings, check evey admin doctor afterwards.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
A theme restyles Evey's interface. It is a package of kind: theme with no backend process, containing:

  • theme.css, a stylesheet injected into every page after sanitization;
  • optionally theme.js, a script run in an isolated frame with a small evey.theme API.

A theme cannot declare language, entrypoint or permissions: the install is refused if it does. Both files are checked at install. Themes are installed like plugins, from Admin → Plugins.

docs.title: Manifest schema
docs.text:
name: aurora               # required; human-readable name
version: 1.0.0             # required; semver
kind: theme                # required; must be "theme"

description: "..."         # optional
author: "..."              # optional
min_evey_version: "1.0.0"  # optional

# NO language, entrypoint, permissions - these are invalid for themes

The ZIP must contain theme.css and/or theme.js at its root. A package with neither is accepted but the theme has no visible effect.

docs.title: theme.css
docs.text:
Served at /api/v1/themes/<id>/theme.css. The file is passed through the CSS sanitizer at install time.

The stylesheet is injected as a <link rel="stylesheet"> in <head>. It applies globally to the host document. Standard CSS applies: custom properties, @keyframes, @media, @font-face (with data: sources), @layer, container queries.

The sanitizer rewrites or removes what a theme may not do and records a warning for each change; it does not refuse the file. What is stored and served is the sanitized output, so it can differ from what you wrote.

docs.title: What the sanitizer removes
docs.text:
@import - removed entirely.

Any @import directive is stripped. Rationale: themes must be self-contained; external stylesheet imports are a network leak vector.

External url() - replaced with none.

url() values pointing to http://, https://, or protocol-relative // URLs are replaced. data: URIs (data:image/*, data:font/*) are allowed and pass through unchanged.

javascript: in url() - replaced with none.

expression() (IE legacy) - replaced with none.

-moz-binding and behavior - removed.

Legacy XBL/HTC execution vectors, removed entirely.

Sensitive selector rules - entire rule block removed.

Rule blocks whose selector matches any of the following are stripped completely:

  • [type="password"] or [type='password'] or [type=password]
  • [type="hidden"]
  • .admin-<anything>
  • .token-<anything>
  • .secret-<anything>

Rationale: themes must not be able to style password inputs or privileged UI elements in ways that could be used for UI redressing.

Full-screen overlay rules - entire rule block removed.

A rule block is removed when it combines position: fixed or position: sticky with a box that covers the screen: inset: 0, the four sides at 0, or at least two of top: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0, left: 0, width: 100vw, height: 100vh including one of the two viewport sizes. A header pinned with top: 0; left: 0 and sized by its content is kept. Declarations for the same selector are added up across rules, so splitting the pattern over several blocks does not escape it. This pattern is the canonical CSS phishing overlay.

pointer-events: none on interactive elements - declaration removed from rule block.

When a rule's selector targets button, [role="button"], a[href*=logout], or [data-critical], any pointer-events: none declaration in that rule is removed. The rest of the rule is kept. Rationale: hiding clickability on logout or critical action buttons is a UI redress attack.

z-index above 999 - clamped to 999.

Any z-index value greater than 999 is rewritten to 999. A warning is recorded. Themes may not stack themselves above the application's own modal/overlay layer.

docs.title: What a theme can do in CSS
docs.text:
• Customize the entire homepage layout, hero area, card grid, sidebar
  • Restyle the video player controls, progress bar, overlays
  • Custom fonts (via data: or inline @font-face with src: url(data:...))
  • Animations and transitions (@keyframes, transition, animation)
  • Custom properties (--my-color: #...), :root overrides
  • Media queries, container queries
  • Any selector that does not target password fields, .admin-*, .token-*, .secret-*

docs.title: Stable theming hooks (selector contract)
docs.text:
Evey marks a small set of cosmetic, non-sensitive elements with stable classes you can target without depending on the (volatile) utility classes. These are a contract: they will not be renamed across refactors.

Selector Element Safe to restyle .evey-app-header the top bar colours, height, spacing, blur - never hide/move the controls inside it .evey-media-grid the media card grids (library, rows) columns, gap, alignment .evey-media-card one media card (poster + meta) width, spacing, hover .evey-poster the poster/artwork visual (also on detail) aspect-ratio, border-radius, shadow, fit .evey-media-detail the media detail page root layout of the detail body

Anything the sanitizer forbids still applies (no @import, no full-screen overlays, no pointer-events:none on controls, no [type=password] / .admin-* / .token-* / .secret-*, z-index clamped). A theme may restyle these hooks freely; it may not repurpose the header to hide or impersonate the trusted controls (logout, profile, real notifications).

docs.title: Example: bigger posters, denser grid, sharper corners
docs.text:
/* Larger posters on a tighter grid */
.evey-media-card { width: 12rem; }
.evey-poster     { border-radius: 2px; }
.evey-media-grid { gap: 0.75rem; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); }

.evey-media-card:hover { transform: scale(1.03); transition: transform 120ms ease; }

docs.title: Example: a different accent colour
docs.text:
The interface draws buttons, links, active states and the player's progress bar from a few custom properties; examples/plugins/theme-dark-blue/theme.css lists them. Overriding them restyles every screen at once:

:root {
  --accent: #e8a33d;
  --accent-hover: #f0b95c;
}

docs.title: theme.js
docs.text:
Served at /api/v1/themes/<id>/theme.js (authentication required). Loaded inside an iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" and a locked Content Security Policy - the script has no access to the host page, cannot make network requests, and cannot read storage.

The only surface available is window.evey.theme, injected by the host bridge before theme.js runs.

Even a script that passed the install scanner cannot reach the host page, its storage or the network: the frame has no same-origin access and its policy sets connect-src 'none'.

docs.title: evey.theme.css(rules)
docs.text:
Injects a CSS string into the host's style surface at runtime. Use for dynamic styling that depends on computed values or user interaction within the theme.

evey.theme.css(`
  .hero-banner {
    background-image: url(data:image/svg+xml,...);
  }
`);

docs.title: evey.theme.log(level, msg)
docs.text:
Emits a log message to the browser console, prefixed [evey-theme]. Does not surface to end users.

  • level: "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error"
  • msg: plain text string
evey.theme.log("info", "Aurora theme loaded.");

docs.title: What the scanner refuses
docs.text: A single match refuses the install, with the reason. The scanner is deliberately conservative: a theme has no legitimate reason to use these APIs.

docs.title: Literal strings
docs.text:
If any of the following substrings appears anywhere in the source, install is refused:

  • document.cookie
  • localStorage
  • sessionStorage
  • indexedDB
  • XMLHttpRequest
  • navigator.sendBeacon
  • navigator.serviceWorker
  • WebSocket
  • EventSource
  • importScripts
  • document.write
  • Element.prototype
  • Object.defineProperty
  • globalThis
  • window.parent
  • window.top
  • window.opener
  • Reflect.get
  • Reflect.apply
  • Reflect.construct
  • window.frames
  • frameElement
  • postMessage

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text: Pattern What it catches \b(fetch\|eval\|atob\|btoa\|Function\|setTimeout\|setInterval)\s*\( Direct calls to forbidden globals \bimport\s*\( Dynamic import (?:window\|self\|globalThis\|top\|parent\|document\|navigator\|location)\s*\[ Bracket-notation access on host globals (catches window["fetch"]) \.cookie\b any .cookie access, property descriptor or computed \.constructor\s*\.\s*constructor [].constructor.constructor escape new\s+Function\b new Function(...) code construction (?:window\|self\|top\|parent\|globalThis)\s*\.\s*(?:Function\|eval\|fetch\|atob\|btoa\|XMLHttpRequest\|WebSocket\|EventSource)\b Property read of forbidden globals (?:window\|top\|parent\|document\|location\|globalThis\|self)\s*\.\s*[A-Za-z_$][\w$]*\s*=[^=] Property assignment to host globals Object\s*\.\s*prototype Prototype pollution \.register\s*\(\s*['"]\S+\.js Service worker registration

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Two themes ship with the plugin examples: examples/plugins/theme-dark-blue (a short theme.css that only overrides colour variables) and examples/plugins/open-workshop (a complete restyle). Copy either as a starting point - both already pass the sanitizer.

docs.title: Webhooks and API keys
docs.text: Two ways to connect Evey to other tools without writing a plugin: webhooks send Evey's events to a URL of yours, API keys let your scripts call Evey.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Admin → Webhooks → Create Webhook: a name, a URL, the events to send, and an optional secret. Test sends a ping and reports the answer.

A webhook sending the start and the end of each playback.

Events. A webhook subscribes to all events or to a chosen list. The events are those of the server itself, for example:

Area Events Library library.scan.started, library.scan.completed, media.item.added, media.item.updated, media.item.removed Playback playback.started, playback.stopped, media.marked.watched, transcode.started, transcode.failed Accounts user.created, user.login.succeeded, user.login.failed, user.profile.created Requests media.request.created, media.request.answered Server backup.created, backup.failed, plugin.installed, plugin.error, server.config.changed

Delivery. Each event is a JSON POST. Two headers come with it:

  • X-Evey-Delivery: an identifier that stays the same across the retries of one delivery, so your receiver can ignore a duplicate;
  • X-Evey-Signature: sha256= followed by the HMAC-SHA256 of the body, computed with the webhook's secret. Verify it with the same secret to know the request comes from your server. Without a secret, the signature proves nothing.

A delivery that fails is retried after 1, 5 and 30 seconds. Each attempt is recorded in the webhook's delivery log.

Only public addresses. A webhook URL must be http or https and point to a public address. Private and local addresses (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x, localhost, a container name that resolves to one) are refused, when the webhook is saved and again when the server connects. This protects the server against being used to reach your internal network; a receiver on your local network needs a public address or a relay.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
An API key lets a script call the server API without a password. Keys are created in Admin → API Keys, by an administrator, and belong to that administrator.

  • The key is shown once, when it is created. Store it then; it cannot be displayed again, only revoked.
  • It acts as its owner, with administrator rights, within its scopes.
  • Scopes restrict what the key can do:
Scope Allows media:read Reading media metadata media:write Modifying media and starting scans playback:read Reading playback state and history playback:write Controlling playback and progress users:read Reading users users:write Modifying users admin:read Reading administration activity and statistics admin:write Modifying administration settings

A key created without any scope has full access, like its owner: this is the legacy behaviour, kept for existing keys. Select the scopes a script needs.

The key goes in the Authorization header, with or without Bearer:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer evey_..." https://media.example.com/api/v1/...

A key stops working at once when it is revoked, or when its owner is disabled. The endpoints themselves are listed in the Server API.

docs.title: Hardware acceleration
docs.text:
A graphics card or an integrated GPU lets the server transcode more streams at once, and higher resolutions, than the processor alone. There is one image for every case: no driver is baked in for a specific card, and the same container runs in software only, with an Intel or AMD GPU, or with an NVIDIA card, depending on the devices you give it.

Two steps: expose the device to the container, then leave Hardware acceleration on Auto in Admin → Transcoding → Encode calibration.

docs.title: Expose the device
docs.text:
Intel / AMD (VAAPI, Quick Sync)NVIDIA (NVENC)Rockchip (RKMPP) docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    devices:
      - /dev/dri:/dev/dri
    group_add:
      - "104"   # the host's render group: getent group render

The group must be the host's render group (getent group render, or stat -c %g /dev/dri/renderD128). A wrong value does not break anything: the GPU is simply not accessible and the server stays on the processor.

Install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host, then reserve the GPU and request the video capability, without which the encoder library is not injected:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    environment:
      NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES: all   # must include "video"
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: all
              capabilities: [gpu]

Map /dev/mpp_service, /dev/dri and, where the kernel exposes it, /dev/rga. See ARM hosts.

Both an NVIDIA reservation and /dev/dri can be mapped at once.

docs.title: What Auto does
docs.text:
With Auto, the server works only from measurements, never from the name of the card:

  1. Detect. Each render node is probed for VAAPI and, on Intel, Quick Sync; each NVIDIA GPU and the Rockchip encoder likewise. An encoder counts only if a real encode succeeds.
  2. Certify. Each accelerator encodes the resolution ladder (720p to 2160p) in the same pipeline shape as real playback, keeps the highest rung it sustains at 1.2 times real time, and passes a visual check. An accelerator that cannot sustain 720p is not used.
  3. Measure the routes. For each capability the accelerator proved (SDR, HEVC, AV1, tone mapping on the GPU, HDR kept), the cost of a real session is measured.
  4. Choose per stream. Each playback goes to the cheapest accelerator that has proved what that stream needs, or to the processor. See Transcoding and server capacity.

The measurement runs at the server's first quiet moment and again after the hardware changes. Recalibrate runs it immediately: use it after adding a card or moving the container to another machine.

Off keeps every transcode on the processor, which is the escape hatch for a faulty driver. Choosing a Backend by hand (NVENC, VAAPI, QSV, RKMPP) forces that one; if it turns out unusable, the server falls back to the processor and the card shows the backend actually in use.

On a machine with several accelerators, Auto has no fixed preference: each is certified and measured, and every stream goes to the backend that proved the route it needs, at the best proven quality and the lowest measured cost. Two streams on the same server can therefore use different backends, for example HDR tone mapping on one card and an HEVC encode on another.

docs.title: Checking that it is used
docs.text:
Admin → Transcoding → Encode calibration shows the accelerators detected, the backend in use, the resolutions certified for the GPU and for the processor, and any fallback to the processor. During playback, Admin → Now Playing names the backend each stream is encoded with.

Under WSL2, NVENC works; VAAPI and Quick Sync do not (the WSL graphics driver fails on these encodes), and the admin panel greys them out.

docs.title: Libraries and metadata
docs.text:
A library is a type and a set of folders. Evey scans the folders, recognises each file from its name, and fetches its metadata: titles, summaries, posters, cast, ratings. Libraries are managed in Admin → Libraries.

Admin → Libraries: one row per library, with its folders, its item count and its last scan.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type Recognised as Metadata from Movies One film per file (or per folder) TMDB, completed by OMDb when a key is set Shows Series, seasons, episodes TMDB Music Artists, albums, tracks The files' tags; covers from the files, the album folder, Cover Art Archive (MusicBrainz), then iTunes Photos Albums, pictures with their shooting details The files

Keep films and series in separate libraries: the type tells the scanner what to look for.

docs.title: Folders are paths inside the container
docs.text: The folder picker lists what the container sees. With the installation's compose file, your media folder is /media, so a folder /srv/media/films on the host is /media/films for Evey. A second mounted folder (/media2) is added the same way.

docs.title: Naming files
docs.text:
The scanner recognises names like these:

/media/films/The Mirror (1999)/The Mirror (1999) 1080p.mkv
/media/films/Lantern.2010.1080p.BluRay.x264.mkv
/media/series/The Outpost/Season 01/The.Outpost.S01E05.720p.mkv
/media/series/Quiet Storm/Quiet.Storm.03x10.mkv

For a film, the year matters most. For an episode, S01E05 or 1x05. Release tags (resolution, source, codec, audio, language tags such as VOSTFR or MULTI, editions such as "Director's Cut") are removed before the search. If your files carry a tag the parser does not know, add it in Admin → Server Config → Parser tokens; it applies from the next scan.

docs.title: Music libraries
docs.text:
The scanner reads MP3, FLAC, M4A, OGG, Opus, WAV and AAC files, and takes each track from its tags: title (the file name when it is missing), artist, album artist, album, year, track and disc numbers, genre. Artists are grouped by album artist, or by artist when that tag is empty.

An album is a folder. Tracks are grouped by the folder they sit in, not by their album tag: two folders sharing one album tag are two albums, and an album split into CD1 and CD2 subfolders shows as two. Keep each album in one folder; its tracks are ordered by disc number, then track number, and the album takes the name most of its tracks carry.

The cover is the picture embedded in the files, otherwise an image in the album folder (cover.jpg, folder.jpg or front.jpg), otherwise Cover Art Archive (found through MusicBrainz), otherwise iTunes.

docs.title: Photo libraries
docs.text: The scanner reads JPEG, PNG, HEIC, WebP, GIF, TIFF and BMP files. A photo's album is its folder, relative to the library folder; a photo at the top level has none, and moving a file to another folder moves it to that album at the next scan. The date taken and the camera model come from the EXIF data of JPEG files; the other formats are listed without them. Thumbnails are resized on the server and kept in the transcoding cache.

docs.title: How new files are picked up
docs.text:
Each library has three options:

Option Effect Realtime monitoring New, renamed and deleted files are picked up as they appear. A periodic check (every 2 minutes by default) catches what the file system did not report, which happens on network shares. Scan on startup A scan each time the server starts. Schedule A full scan every 6 or 12 hours, daily, weekly, or on a cron expression.

The server also checks that its folder watcher still receives events, by writing a probe file into the library folder for a few seconds. A library where events stop arriving is walked more often until the watcher recovers.

docs.title: When a title is wrong or missing
docs.text:
• Match orphans only (per library) retries the files that were never recognised. It is fast.
  • Re-match all from TMDB redoes the search for every title in the library. It is slow, and corrects old mistakes after a large renaming.
  • Edit Metadata on a title changes its details by hand, or pastes the right TMDB or IMDb id. A value you edit is kept: later refreshes do not overwrite it. Re-match metadata on the title discards your edits and searches again from the file name.
  • Repair sagas joins films that belong to no collection back to their saga, when the other films of the saga are already in the library.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Collections gathers titles under one name, for every account. There are three kinds:

  • TMDB Collections: the sagas, filled in on their own when TMDB places a film in one. Repair sagas (above) catches films that missed theirs.
  • New collection: a list an administrator fills by hand, with Add to Collection on a title or on a selection, and puts in order.
  • New smart collection: rules on Genre, Year, Type, Rating ≥ and Library, which a title must all meet. Its content is worked out each time it is opened, so new titles appear without doing anything.

Only administrators create and edit collections. Anyone can browse them, and Download collection on the web gets the original files as one ZIP (up to 1000 titles), leaving out what the account's library access or age limit hides.

docs.title: Metadata keys
docs.text:
Evey ships with a TMDB key, so metadata works without configuration. Other sources are optional; their keys go in Admin → Server Config → API Keys, and a key set there wins over the same key given in the environment.

Key Adds TMDB (your own) Your own request quota instead of the shared one. OMDb A second source for films TMDB knows little about. OpenSubtitles Searching and downloading subtitles a file does not carry, through the server API (the apps do not offer it yet). See Subtitles. TheIntroDB Intro, recap and credits timings from a community database: 500 lookups a day with a key instead of 100 without.

docs.title: Intro, recap and credits
docs.text:
Evey marks the intro, the recap and the credits of episodes and films so the players can offer to skip them. The timings come from community databases (TheIntroDB, then IntroDB) when they know the title, and from the server's own analysis of the files otherwise. An administrator can adjust the segments of a title by hand, or run the detection again.

Players show Skip Intro, Skip Recap and Skip Credits buttons by default. Auto-skip intros (Admin → Server Config → Server Settings, off by default) makes every player skip them on its own.

docs.title: Remote access and HTTPS
docs.text: Reaching the server from outside the home involves two separate things: a public HTTPS address in front of Evey, and Evey's own remote-access setting, which decides whether clients outside your network are served.

docs.title: Remote access is decided from the public address
docs.text:
Evey decides remote access at startup unless you have chosen it yourself:

  • if the server was given a public address (EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL or EVEY_REMOTE_ACCESS_EXTERNAL_URL), remote access is on;
  • otherwise it is off, and only clients on your local networks are served.

Once you change the setting in Admin → Remote Access, your choice is kept and the server no longer infers it: a published server can stay LAN-only if that is what you want.

When remote access is off, a client outside the local networks receives a 403 on every page, and the apps show a message saying remote access is disabled rather than a generic error. If the server is reachable from the internet while remote access is off, the admin page shows Every remote user is locked out, the server logs it at startup and logs each refusal with the client address, and evey admin doctor reports it as a failure.

Remote access is a choice about who may reach the server, not a protection: every page still requires signing in.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Admin → Remote Access. Every setting applies without a restart: the network ones to the next request, the bitrate to the next playback.

A server published at an https:// address behind a proxy on the Docker network. Setting Effect Enable Remote Access On: clients outside the local networks are served like any other. Off: they get a 403. External URL The public address. E-mail links, single sign-on redirects and cast URLs are built from it. An https:// address also turns on HTTPS mode (below). Trusted proxies The reverse proxies whose forwarded client address Evey believes. Loopback is always trusted. Empty: the list comes from EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES. LAN Networks The address ranges treated as home. Private ranges are listed by default. Add a VPN range (Tailscale, WireGuard) here if its clients should count as home. Max Remote Bitrate A bitrate ceiling for clients outside the local networks, in kbit/s (0 = none). A private address is never capped. When Admin → Transcoding also sets a ceiling for remote viewers, the lower of the two applies. See How playback is decided.

docs.title: HTTPS: a reverse proxy in front of Evey
docs.text:
Evey serves plain HTTP on port 9091, API and web interface together. HTTPS is the job of a reverse proxy, which forwards everything to evey-server:9091. Evey needs to know two things about it, both in Admin → Remote Access:

  • External URL in https://. This is what tells Evey a proxy terminates TLS: cookies get the Secure flag, HSTS is sent and the X-Forwarded-Proto header of a trusted proxy is believed.
  • Trusted proxies, when the proxy is not on the same machine as Evey. A proxy in another container needs its network here, for example 172.16.0.0/12 for Docker's default networks. A range covering every address (0.0.0.0/0, ::/0) is refused: any client could then choose the address it is seen with.

With no proxy yet, Evey's repository provides a Caddy service that obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate on its own. Ready-made configurations for Caddy, Nginx, Traefik and Nginx Proxy Manager, and what a proxy's defaults do to streaming: Reverse proxy configurations.

docs.title: Setting it in the environment instead
docs.text: EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL and EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES give the same answers from the compose file, which suits an installation described entirely as code or a server that must be reachable over HTTPS from its very first start. The panel wins when both are set: an https:// External URL enables HTTPS mode even if the base URL is plain HTTP, and a saved proxy list replaces the variable. Emptying the field hands the answer back to the variable. See Server and network.

docs.title: The two network steps
docs.text: Trusted proxies and LAN networks are two successive steps, not two ways of saying the same thing. The trusted proxies decide whose forwarded address is believed, and so which address each client gets; the LAN networks then classify that address as local or remote.

docs.title: The real client address
docs.text:
Remote access and Max Remote Bitrate both depend on Evey seeing each client's real address. A proxy that does not forward it, or that Evey does not trust, makes every request look like it comes from the proxy's private address: everyone counts as home, the remote-access setting has no effect and no remote cap applies.

Fixing the proxy therefore changes who counts as remote. If remote access was off, remote clients are refused from that moment. Check evey admin doctor after changing proxy settings: it names the list in force and where it comes from, warns about a public range and fails on a range covering every address.

docs.title: Accounts and profiles
docs.text: An account signs in: it has a username and a password (or a single sign-on identity, see OIDC), and it is either an administrator or not. A profile watches: each account holds one or more profiles, each with its own watch history, resume points, favourites, languages and home page. A household typically shares one account, with a profile per person.

docs.title: Creating accounts
docs.text:
Admin → Users offers two ways:

Admin → Users: each account with its profiles, its role and its state.
  • Create User: you choose the username and the password.
  • Create Invite Link: the person chooses their own. A link can have an expiry date and a maximum number of uses, restrict the libraries the new account sees, cap the number of profiles it may create, and create an administrator. Invite Links lists them; a link can be revoked.

docs.title: What an administrator can restrict per account
docs.text:
Setting Effect Library Access The libraries the account sees. Everything else is absent from its searches, home page and API responses. Max Bitrate A ceiling on the bitrate the account's players receive (0 = unlimited). A title above it is transcoded down to it. Max profiles How many profiles the account may create (0 = unlimited). Max devices per profile How many playbacks each profile may have running at once, across its devices (0 = unlimited). One more is refused when it starts.

Connect as opens the server as that user sees it, to check a restriction or reproduce a problem. A banner stays visible, and Exit returns to your own account.

docs.title: Kids profiles and the PIN
docs.text:
A profile marked Kids profile opens without a PIN. Leaving it for a profile that is not a kids profile asks for the 4-digit PIN, set in Settings → Parental. Setting the PIN the first time asks for the account password, and while a kids profile exists the account must have a PIN.

Managing profiles and parental settings is only possible from a profile that is not a kids profile.

docs.title: Age limits
docs.text:
Each profile can have a Max age rating (Settings → Profiles → Edit). The rating system is the one of the country set in Admin → Server Config → Language & Region.

The limit is applied by the server, not by the apps: a title above it is not hidden in the interface, it is never sent. That holds for browsing and search, for playback and for downloads. If the server cannot read a profile's settings (a database error, for example), it refuses the content rather than allowing it. Administrators are not subject to profile limits.

A film downloaded to a phone stays subject to the limit offline: a kids profile cannot open a download made by another profile above its age limit.

docs.title: Opening hours
docs.text:
A kids profile can be limited to opening hours: the clock icon next to it in the profile list (Settings → Profiles, or the user's page in Admin → Users) opens the editor. Nothing is set until you turn it on; the editor then suggests weekdays 18:00 to 22:00, and Saturday and Sunday 9:00 to 12:00 and 14:00 to 21:00.

The hours are a list of time ranges, edited two ways: Weekdays / weekend (one block for Monday to Friday, one for the weekend) or Day by day. A day can have several ranges, a range can run past midnight (20:00 to 0:30), and a day with no range is closed. Switching back to the week view is refused when the days of a block differ, so nothing is lost silently.

The server enforces the hours, in its own time zone (Admin → Server Config → Language & Region → Server time zone; without it, the TZ variable, then Europe/Paris). Changing the clock of a tablet changes nothing. Outside the hours the profile is refused everywhere - browsing, every segment of a film in progress, music, downloads - and every app shows a lock screen saying when it opens again. Ten minutes before closing, the player shows a warning; at the time, playback stops.

On the lock screen, the PIN of an adult profile of the same account opens the kids profile until its next opening; the child's own PIN, if it has one, does not. Switch profile leads to the profile picker. A schedule that the server cannot read keeps the profile closed rather than open.

A film downloaded to a phone and played without a connection does not reach the server, so the hours do not apply to it.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text: Users can search for a film, a series or an artist that is missing from the libraries and ask for it. Requests arrive in Admin → Media Requests, where an administrator approves, declines or postpones them, with a note. Who may request is set there: everyone by default, with per-user exceptions.

docs.title: Public download links
docs.text:
On a film or episode page, an administrator can create a Public download link (web and Android apps). It is a URL anyone can open, without an account, to download the original file; it is copied to the clipboard.

  • It expires after 48 hours. Through the server API it can last up to 72 hours and be limited to a number of downloads (POST /api/v1/media/{id}/share).
  • Only administrators can create, list and revoke links. The apps only create them: listing and revoking go through the API (GET /api/v1/admin/share-links, DELETE /api/v1/share-links/{id}).
  • With remote access off, the link only works from the local networks.
  • Whoever holds the link can download the file until it expires: share it like the file itself.

docs.title: The home page
docs.text:
The home page is a stack of rows; a row with nothing to show is hidden.

Row What it shows Resume Playback What the profile started and has not finished, most recent first. A title counts as watched at 90 %. Up Next For each series the profile has watched an episode of, the next unwatched episode. Collections The collections, with a link to the full list. Recommended For You Films and series in the profile's usual genres, best match first, then by rating. A genre counts when it appears in at least 3 of the profile's last 200 playbacks. Most Popular The films and series played most on the server over the last 90 days. One row per library The latest additions to that library, newest first.

Recommended For You and Most Popular leave out what the profile has already finished; a series counts as finished once every episode is watched. Plugins can add their own rows.

Admin → Server Config → Home feeds sets the default for every profile: which rows appear, in what order, and how many items each shows. Each profile then arranges its own home with Customize (on the home page of the web and mobile apps, in the header of the TV app): show or hide a row, move it, or Reset to Defaults. The choice is saved on the server and follows the profile to every device. A profile can show a row the administrator has hidden, except a plugin's row: there the administrator's choice is final.

docs.title: Evey API Documentation
docs.text: OpenAPI (Swagger 2.0) specifications for the Evey media server.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: Section Description Public API User-facing endpoints - media browsing, playback, collections, playlists, etc. Admin API Server administration - system config, transcoding, backups, metadata, etc. Plugin API Plugin management and webhook integrations.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Each folder contains individual .swagger.json files that can be imported into any OpenAPI-compatible tool (Swagger UI, Postman, Insomnia, etc.).

docs.title: Regeneration
docs.text:
These specs are generated from protobuf definitions via buf generate. To update:

buf generate --template buf.gen.local.yaml
python3 docs/api/sync.py

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text: Administrative endpoints restricted to users with admin privileges.

docs.title: System
docs.text: Spec Description admin_system.swagger.json Dashboard, system info, setup wizard server_config.swagger.json Server configuration key/value store remote_access.swagger.json Remote access and network settings backup.swagger.json Database backup and restore backup_schedule.swagger.json Scheduled backups: cron, retention, run now activity.swagger.json Play history, login history, server metrics admin_session.swagger.json Audit log admin_task.swagger.json Scheduled background tasks presence.swagger.json Who is connected right now (the apps' heartbeat and the admin list)

docs.title: Media & Transcoding
docs.text: Spec Description admin_media.swagger.json Media health (scans, repairs, history and undo), delete media items, refresh metadata, generate trickplay metadata.swagger.json Metadata providers, search, overrides transcoding.swagger.json Transcode profiles, hardware detection, active jobs transcode_cache.swagger.json Transcode cache management mkv.swagger.json MKV container tools (tracks, chapters, mux/demux) admin_intro.swagger.json Intro timing cache: invalidate one episode, backfill

docs.title: Users & Policies
docs.text: Spec Description library_access.swagger.json Per-user library access control parental.swagger.json Parental controls and PIN playback_settings.swagger.json Global playback settings

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Every endpoint needs an administrator: the session token of an administrator account, or an API key, which always belongs to one (its scopes can narrow it).

docs.title: Plugin API
docs.text: Endpoints for managing plugins and webhook integrations.

docs.title: Specs
docs.text: Spec Description admin_plugin.swagger.json Install, enable, disable, uninstall plugins. Plugin config and logs. Plugin runtimes. webhook.swagger.json CRUD webhooks, delivery history plugin_prefs.swagger.json A plugin interface's per-user preferences (the prefs permission)

docs.title: Plugin Development
docs.text: Plugins communicate with the Evey server via gRPC. See Plugin Documentation for the full development guide including: - Plugin lifecycle (install, enable, configure, disable, uninstall) - Available event hooks - Configuration schema - Security sandboxing (seccomp, process isolation)

docs.title: Public API
docs.text: User-facing endpoints available to all authenticated users.

docs.title: Specs
docs.text: Spec Description library.swagger.json Libraries, media items, search, people playback.swagger.json Streaming, progress tracking, watch history, resume user.swagger.json Authentication, profiles, API keys, Quick Connect collection.swagger.json Smart and manual collections favorite.swagger.json Favorite items feed.swagger.json Home feed sections (continue watching, recently added, etc.) playlist.swagger.json Playlists, made by hand or by rules rating.swagger.json User ratings share.swagger.json Public share links syncplay.swagger.json Synchronized playback rooms notification.swagger.json In-app notifications push.swagger.json Web push subscriptions music.swagger.json Music library (artists, albums, tracks) photo.swagger.json Photo library (albums, photos) media_request.swagger.json Media requests: search, submit, policy; the administrator's answers and request access

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Endpoints take Authorization: Bearer <token>: a session token from signing in, or an API key (see Webhooks and API keys). Open without one: signing in and renewing a session, signing up with an invitation, Quick Connect, password reset, the setup wizard and its status, and public download links.

docs.title: Accounts and sign-in
docs.text: Session lifetimes, the signing key, and single sign-on.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: Variable Default Effect EVEY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH /data/jwt.key The key that signs access tokens, generated on the first start. If it is lost, the next start generates a new one and the apps renew their tokens: nobody is signed out. EVEY_JWT_ACCESS_TTL 15m Lifetime of an access token. Apps renew it silently. EVEY_JWT_REFRESH_TTL 168h (7 days) Lifetime of a sign-in session: without using an app for that long, you sign in again. EVEY_JWT_REFRESH_LONG_TTL 4320h (180 days) Lifetime of a session an app asks to keep, such as a TV signed in with Quick Connect.

docs.title: Single sign-on (OIDC)
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect EVEY_OIDC_ENABLED false Turns single sign-on on. EVEY_OIDC_ISSUER empty The provider's issuer URL, for example https://auth.example.com/realms/main. EVEY_OIDC_CLIENT_ID empty The client registered for Evey at the provider. EVEY_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET empty Its secret. EVEY_OIDC_REDIRECT_URL empty The callback address sent to the provider: https://<your address>/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback. Empty: built from the server's public address (Admin → Remote Access). EVEY_OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS empty (all) E-mail domains allowed to sign in, comma-separated. The provider must have verified the address. EVEY_OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP empty true or false: create accounts for new SSO users. Empty: on only when e-mail domains are set.

These are the fallback: each setting saved in the Single sign-on (SSO) card of Admin → Server Config replaces its variable, without a restart. Setting up a provider: Single sign-on (OIDC).

docs.title: Background work
docs.text: The passes the server runs on its own, and how they share the processor. How they behave: Background work and server load.

docs.title: CPU share
docs.text:
The share of the processor background tasks may use is set in Admin → Server Config → Processing power, live, without a restart. It has no environment variable. The two below size a pool by hand and bypass that share for it:

Variable Default Effect EVEY_LIBRARY_SCAN_WORKERS from the share Files analysed in parallel during a scan. EVEY_INTRO_DETECTION_MAX_PARALLEL from the share Titles analysed at once for intros and credits.

docs.title: Passes
docs.text:
Each variable has a key, also accepted as a row in Admin → Server Config → Config entries, which suggests these keys; the row wins. All are read at startup, and Background work in the same screen sets the main ones.

Variable Panel key Default Effect EVEY_TRANSCODING_PAUSE_BG_ON_PLAYBACK transcoding.pause_bg_on_playback on Pauses background work while a stream plays. off keeps it running. EVEY_KEYFRAME_BACKFILL transcoding.keyframe_backfill on Indexes the keyframes of scanned files and classifies their frame rate. Direct Play and copy depend on it. off disables it. EVEY_KEYFRAME_BACKFILL_BATCH transcoding.keyframe_backfill_batch server default Files per pass (> 0). EVEY_KEYFRAME_BACKFILL_PAUSE_MS transcoding.keyframe_backfill_pause_ms server default Milliseconds between files (>= 0). EVEY_KEYFRAME_BACKFILL_IDLE_SEC transcoding.keyframe_backfill_idle_sec server default Seconds between passes when idle (> 0). EVEY_LEVEL_BACKFILL transcoding.level_backfill on Reads the H.264/HEVC level of files scanned before it was collected. off disables it. EVEY_LEVEL_BACKFILL_BATCH, _PAUSE_MS, _IDLE_SEC transcoding.level_backfill_batch, _pause_ms, _idle_sec server default Same pacing, for this pass. EVEY_SNAPSHOT_FASTPATH transcoding.snapshot_fastpath on Extracts thumbnails with the fast in-process decoder. off uses the exact ffmpeg extractor only, to rule it out when a thumbnail shows the wrong frame. EVEY_TITLE_PROBE transcoding.title_probe on Probes titles in the background at low priority, paused during playback. off disables it.

docs.title: Database and search
docs.text: By default the image runs its own Postgres and Meilisearch and generates their passwords: none of these variables is needed. They serve an installation that brings its own database or search engine, or tunes the embedded ones. See Advanced deployments.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Variable Default Effect EVEY_EMBEDDED_POSTGRES unset Unset: embedded when EVEY_DB_HOST is unset, external otherwise. true or false to decide explicitly. Read by the entrypoint. EVEY_POSTGRES_DATA_DIR /data/postgres Where the embedded cluster lives. It must be on a local filesystem, not a network share. EVEY_DB_HOST localhost The database host. Setting it turns the embedded database off. EVEY_DB_PORT 5432 The database port. EVEY_DB_USER evey The database login. When it is a superuser (the embedded cluster and the shipped compose), the server keeps it for the restore only and runs as EVEY_DB_APP_USER. EVEY_DB_APP_USER evey_app The unprivileged role the server and its migrations run as when EVEY_DB_USER is a superuser. Created at boot, handed the database and its objects, given a new random password on every boot (never written anywhere). An SQL injection then cannot run programs or read files on the host. EVEY_DB_PRIVILEGE_SPLIT true false runs everything as EVEY_DB_USER, superuser included. A way out if a database refuses the split; the boot otherwise stops and names this variable. EVEY_DB_NAME evey The database name. EVEY_DB_PASSWORD generated The password. With an external database the server refuses to start on the value evey. EVEY_DB_PASSWORD_FILE /data/keys/postgres.password A file holding the password, read when EVEY_DB_PASSWORD is unset. Set by the image. EVEY_DB_SSLMODE disable on loopback, prefer otherwise disable, prefer, require or verify-full. EVEY_DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS 25 Open connections to the database. Each costs memory on the Postgres side; raise it only for a large deployment. EVEY_DB_MAX_IDLE_CONNS 10 Connections kept idle in the pool.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Variable Default Effect EVEY_EMBEDDED_MEILI true false uses the Meilisearch at EVEY_MEILI_URL instead of the embedded one. Read by the entrypoint. EVEY_MEILI_URL http://localhost:7700 The Meilisearch address. MEILI_MASTER_KEY generated The Meilisearch key. With an external instance, an empty or placeholder key refuses the start. MEILI_MASTER_KEY_FILE /data/keys/meili.key A file holding the key, read when MEILI_MASTER_KEY is unset. Set by the image. MEILI_MAX_INDEXING_MEMORY about 20 % of the container's memory, at least 128 MiB The memory the embedded Meilisearch may use for indexing. Computed from the container limit, not the machine's memory, so a scan does not exhaust a small container. An explicit value is passed through.

docs.title: Libraries and metadata
docs.text: Scanning, metadata sources and intro detection. Most of these have a counterpart in the admin panel, which wins once a value is saved there.

docs.title: Scanning
docs.text: Variable Default Effect EVEY_LIBRARY_WATCHER_ENABLED true Realtime file watching. EVEY_LIBRARY_PERIODIC_SCAN_INTERVAL 2m How often the folders are checked for what the watcher missed (network shares). Admin → Server Config → Server Settings overrides it. EVEY_LIBRARY_SCAN_WORKERS from the CPU share Files analysed in parallel during a scan. Set by hand, it bypasses the Processing power share for scans. EVEY_SEEKINDEX_STATE_DIR /data/seek-index Where the Media health scan keeps its results and its running job across restarts. Empty: not kept.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: Variable Default Effect EVEY_METADATA_LANGUAGE en The language of titles and summaries. The language chosen in the setup wizard or in Admin → Server Config → Language & Region wins. EVEY_TMDB_API_KEY built-in key Your own TMDB key, for your own quota. The key set in Admin → Server Config → API Keys wins. EVEY_OMDB_API_KEY empty An OMDb key, a second source for films. Same override. EVEY_OPENSUBTITLES_API_KEY empty An OpenSubtitles key, for subtitle search through the API. Same override. EVEY_OPENSUBTITLES_USERNAME, EVEY_OPENSUBTITLES_PASSWORD empty An OpenSubtitles account, used to sign in to its API.

docs.title: Intro, recap and credits
docs.text: Variable Default Effect EVEY_INTRO_PROVIDERS_ENABLED false Uses the community databases (TheIntroDB, then IntroDB) before the server's own detection. Admin → Server Config → Intro Skip Providers wins; restart after changing it. EVEY_INTRO_TIDB_API_KEY empty A TheIntroDB key: 500 lookups a day instead of 100. EVEY_INTRO_AUTO_SKIP_ENABLED false Every player skips detected intros on its own. Applies live from the panel. EVEY_INTRO_SKIP_PREVIEW_ENABLED false Also offers to skip the preview of the next episode. Applies live from the panel. EVEY_INTRO_DETECTION_MAX_PARALLEL from the CPU share Titles analysed at once. Set by hand, it bypasses the Processing power share for this task. EVEY_INTRO_FFMPEG_THREADS 1 Threads per ffmpeg process during detection (1 to 16).
