docs.text: The plugin may read media records and streams. Maps to the media.read permission in the manifest.

docs.title: media.write
docs.text: The plugin may create or update media records. Maps to the media.write permission.

docs.title: notification.sender
docs.text: The plugin may publish notifications. The host routes outbound notification events through the plugin. Maps to the notification.sender permission.

docs.title: webhook.receiver
docs.text: The plugin registers as a webhook endpoint. The host forwards matching inbound HTTP POST requests to the plugin via gRPC. No additional permission required beyond the capability declaration.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: public and prefs are permissions, not capabilities - they don't change which server-side role the plugin fulfills, they grant the plugin's iframe extra read/write scopes. Declare them under permissions in the manifest.

docs.title: public
docs.text: Grants the plugin's iframe read-only access to non-sensitive server data: GetPublicMediaItem / ListPublicMediaItems, which return a safe projection (id, title, type, year, overview, poster URL) - never file paths, sizes, provider ids or streams. Server branding (name) is already public and needs no permission. Declare public in permissions to request it.

docs.title: prefs
docs.text:
Grants the plugin's iframe read/write of the current user's preferences in the plugin's own namespace, via PluginUserDataService (GetPref / SetPref / DeletePref / ListPrefs). The plugin and user are bound by the iframe token, so a plugin can only touch (its-own-plugin, the-current-user) data - never another plugin's, never another user's, never identity/security fields. Rows cascade-delete with the plugin or the user. Declare prefs in permissions.

What you can never request. admin.*, auth.* (login/logout/session), system.*, and generic user.write / library.write are hard-locked: they are stripped from any token and rejected at the API boundary even if a manifest tries to declare them. A scoped plugin token is deny-by-default on the server API - it can only reach the methods the granted permissions above explicitly unlock.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: examples/plugins/ holds working plugins in the current manifest format: starters in Node.js and Python (nodejs-example, python-example), a metadata provider (metadata-example), a webhook receiver (webhook-receiver), a home widget (weather), plugin configuration and secrets (config-demo), the data store with the public / prefs permissions and the admin.nav slot (data-demo), and two themes. dev-setup.md walks through copying one.

docs.title: Plugin developer setup
docs.text: End-to-end walkthrough for someone who has just cloned Evey and wants to write, test, and ship a plugin or theme. Pick the runtime that matches your plugin language; the rest is shared.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text: Evey runs the host process (Go) and ships plugins as ZIPs. The plugin runtime depends on what your code calls.

docs.title: Always required
docs.text:
Tool Why Install Go ≥ 1.27 Build the Evey host https://go.dev/dl/ Docker + Docker Compose Default dev stack (Postgres, Meilisearch, server, web) https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ bubblewrap (bwrap) Sandbox for plugin processes - required for the bubblewrap and strict modes apt install bubblewrap (Debian/Ubuntu), dnf install bubblewrap (Fedora), pacman -S bubblewrap (Arch). macOS: install Linux in a VM, bwrap is Linux-only.

The basic sandbox mode runs without bwrap but should never be used outside throwaway local experiments - drop it as soon as you can.

docs.title: Per language
docs.text:
Pick what your plugin actually uses; you don't need them all.

Plugin language Tools Notes Python 3 python3, pip Use pip install --user to keep host clean. SDK stubs live in sdk/python/. Node.js Node 20+, npm or pnpm SDK loads plugin_api.proto at runtime via @grpc/proto-loader. Go Go ≥ 1.21 No bundled stubs - generate with protoc-gen-go + protoc-gen-go-grpc; a compiled Go binary also needs the native-binary permission. Dart / Java / PHP / Ruby / Swift Per-language toolchain Stubs are pre-generated in sdk/<lang>/. CSS-only theme Nothing extra A theme is a ZIP with kind: theme + a theme.css. Theme JS Nothing extra (the host runs your JS inside a sandboxed iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" and a locked-down CSP) The static scanner refuses cookies, storage, network calls and access to the host page (document.cookie, localStorage, fetch(, window.parent...) - see Themes.

docs.title: Generating stubs for another language
docs.text:
Stubs ship pre-generated for the languages above, but the plugin gRPC contract is just a proto file - you can target any language protoc supports (Rust, C#, Kotlin, Elixir, …). The single source of truth is:

proto/plugin/v1/plugin_api.proto

Generate with protoc (or buf), pointing your language's gRPC plugin at it:

# generic shape - exact --*_out flags depend on the language/plugin
protoc --proto_path=proto \
       --<lang>_out=OUT_DIR --grpc_<lang>_out=OUT_DIR \
       proto/plugin/v1/plugin_api.proto

Worked recipes for the bundled languages (which gRPC plugin each needs: grpc_php_plugin, protoc-gen-grpc-java, protoc-gen-grpc-swift, …) live in the plugin-sdk target of the root Makefile and in each sdk/<lang>/README.md (e.g. sdk/php/README.md). make plugin-sdk regenerates the shipped stubs.

Vendor the generated stubs inside your plugin ZIP - the host only auto-copies stubs for the languages it ships (sdk/<lang>/).

docs.title: Optional but recommended
docs.text: Tool Why cosign (Sigstore) Sign your plugin ZIP. EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY defaults to warn (not off) - with warn and no public key configured, verification is a no-op (a warning is logged, nothing is blocked); set EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY to actually verify signatures, and the policy to enforce to refuse unsigned uploads (enforce without a public key stops the server at startup rather than accept every plugin unverified). https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/installation/ pre-commit Catch obvious issues before submitting a plugin. golangci-lint Required if your plugin is in Go and you want linting parity with the host.

docs.title: 2. Bring up Evey locally
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:Evey-project/evey.git
cd evey
cp .env.dev.example .env.dev   # generates a sane local config
make dev                        # docker compose up: postgres, meilisearch, server (Air), web (Vite)

When the server is healthy, browse to https://evey.test (Caddy serves it). The setup wizard creates the administrator account on first launch, as described in First setup.

If make dev fails on bwrap: - Confirm which bwrap returns a path on the host - Inside Docker, the dev container ships the bwrap binary; if you customised the Compose stack, bind-mount it or set EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=basic for the dev container only

docs.title: 3. Scaffold your first plugin
docs.text:
Examples live in examples/plugins/: starters in Node.js and Python (nodejs-example, python-example), a metadata provider (metadata-example), a webhook receiver (webhook-receiver), a home widget (weather), plugin configuration (config-demo) and two themes (theme-dark-blue, open-workshop). Pick the closest one to your use case and copy it into a working directory. For the persistence + permission features, see examples/plugins/data-demo - it uses the per-plugin data store and requests the public / prefs permissions + the admin.nav slot.

cp -r examples/plugins/nodejs-example ~/my-first-plugin
cd ~/my-first-plugin

Edit plugin.yaml:

  • name: kebab-case, unique
  • version: semver - bump on every release
  • kind: plugin (backend required) or theme (frontend-only)
  • language: python | nodejs | go | php | ruby | lua | bash | sh (manifest identifier - not the interpreter binary name; python3/node are not valid language values, see entrypoint below).
  • entrypoint: command line the runtime executes
  • permissions: declare every host API you call. The installer rejects calls that aren't declared. See the permissions catalog for the exhaustive list.
  • external_fetch: when you need to talk to a third-party API. Entries are bare hostnames (api.example.com) - no scheme required or used (any https:// prefix is parsed and only the hostname is kept), no wildcards (*.example.com is rejected at install: external_fetch entry %q is a wildcard - use explicit hostnames), no literal IP addresses (all of them, not just RFC1918). The validator lives in internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/manifest.go (validateExternalFetch); its test coverage is in internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/manifest_test.go - run go test ./internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/... to check your value matches.

Frontend module (optional for kind: plugin, banned for kind: theme):

plugin.yaml
frontend:
  - slot: home.section
    src: dist/index.js

The slot must exist in internal/domain/plugin/slots.go (home.section, home.hero, library.sidebar, media.detail.sidebar, player.overlay, sidebar.bottom, settings.user.appearance, and admin.nav - the one controlled admin-area slot, a menu entry opening your plugin's own sandboxed page). Anything else (admin.* injection, login.*, setup.*, profile.security.*) is rejected at install time.

Storing data. Your backend gets a private key/value store over the host socket (SetData/GetData/DeleteData/ListDataKeys) - no permission needed, wiped automatically on uninstall. For per-user preferences from your iframe, request the prefs permission; for read-only access to non-sensitive media (title/poster), request public. See the API reference. Admin, auth, system and generic write scopes can never be requested.

docs.title: 4. Run the install loop
docs.text:
# zip your plugin
cd ~/my-first-plugin
zip -r my-first-plugin.zip . -x ".*" "node_modules/*" "*.pyc"

# upload through the admin UI
open https://evey.test/admin/plugins
# or via the API
curl -F "plugin=@my-first-plugin.zip" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $EVEY_TOKEN" \
     https://evey.test/api/v1/admin/plugins/upload
# a signature goes in a second field: -F "sig=@my-first-plugin.zip.sig"
# an update that asks for new permissions: -F "accept_permission_changes=true"

The installer runs in this order - every step can refuse the install:

  1. Manifest validation - plugin.yaml parsed straight out of the ZIP (before any ZIP-level checks below), schema-checked. Slot whitelist. Permission/capability whitelist. external_fetch parser (rejects wildcards and any literal IP address; a scheme prefix like http:// is accepted but ignored - only the hostname is kept). The declared language runtime must be available in the image.
  2. Permission escalation (update only) - the installer compares the new manifest against the previous version. Any newly-requested permission/capability/slot/external_fetch host blocks the install with an error the caller must explicitly override (accept_permission_changes: true from the frontend). Fresh installs skip this step - there's nothing to compare against.
  3. Cosign signature - verified when a signature verifier is configured; a failure only blocks the install when EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY=enforce. See section 6.
  4. ZIP extraction - extension, total size ≤ 500 MB, per-entry size ≤ 100 MB, compression ratio ≤ 100:1, no symlinks, no path-traversal entries; files land in a staging dir (upgrades never touch the live version until every later step passes).
  5. CSS sanitizer (themes only) - strips @import, blocks url() non-data:, blocks fullscreen overlays, blocks selectors targeting [type=password] and .admin-*, clamps z-index ≤ 999.
  6. Theme JS scanner (themes only) - refuses any reference to document.cookie, localStorage, fetch, eval, globalThis, bracket-notation property access on host globals, constructor.constructor, etc. Themes must use only the evey.theme.* API.
  7. Static analyzer - scans every text file for shell exec, reverse shell, eval, base64-decode-then-exec, obfuscation patterns, runtime install commands, privilege escalation. Critical findings = refuse install. Warning findings (deserialization, obfuscation, native_code) escalate to refuse unless the matching permission is declared.
  8. Persist - swaps the staging dir into place, writes the row in Postgres, optionally launches the runtime.

If any step fails, the admin UI shows the exact reason. Server logs (docker compose logs evey) carry the full stack.

docs.title: 5. Iterate
docs.text:
Hot-reload your plugin while developing:

# edit code → re-zip → re-upload via UI (Update button)
# or, faster: drop the file directly into the plugin directory inside the container
docker compose exec evey ls /data/plugins/<plugin-id>/

An upload is accepted as an update only when its version is higher than the installed one: bump it on every iteration (a same or lower version is refused), or uninstall first. If you add a new permission, you'll hit the escalation flow - that's the design, not a bug.

Logs from the plugin process land in: - /admin/plugins/<id> - last N lines via the UI - docker compose logs evey | grep <plugin-id> - full stream

docs.title: 6. Sign your plugin (optional in dev, recommended for distribution)
docs.text:
What a signature proves

A signature says the ZIP the admin is installing is byte for byte the one you published, and that it was signed with the key they trust. It says nothing about what the plugin does: the permissions, the hosts and the analysis of the preview still apply. Evey checks it offline and in process (ECDSA P-256 over the SHA-256 of the ZIP, the format cosign sign-blob --key produces): no cosign binary on the server, no network, no transparency log.

You need cosign on your machine only.

1. Once: generate a key pair.

# choose a real passphrase; cosign.key stays private, never commit it
COSIGN_PASSWORD="your-passphrase" cosign generate-key-pair
# -> cosign.key (private) and cosign.pub (the file you hand out)

2. At each release: zip, then sign. The manifest sits at the root of the ZIP. Sign offline, to match how the server verifies:

cd my-first-plugin && zip -r ../my-first-plugin.zip . && cd ..

COSIGN_PASSWORD="your-passphrase" cosign sign-blob \
  --key cosign.key --tlog-upload=false --yes \
  --output-signature my-first-plugin.zip.sig \
  my-first-plugin.zip

3. Check it before shipping, with the same verification the server does:

cosign verify-blob --key cosign.pub --signature my-first-plugin.zip.sig \
  --insecure-ignore-tlog my-first-plugin.zip      # -> Verified OK

4. Publish three files together: my-first-plugin.zip, my-first-plugin.zip.sig and cosign.pub. Put the public key's fingerprint somewhere your users can compare it (README, release notes), so they know cosign.pub was not swapped.

On the instance that installs it:

# put the public key somewhere the server can read
sudo cp cosign.pub /etc/evey/cosign.pub

export EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY=/etc/evey/cosign.pub
export EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY=warn   # or "enforce" to refuse what does not verify
docker compose restart evey

Then, in Admin → Plugins, choose the ZIP and, in the Signature file field, its .zip.sig. Through the API, the signature is the optional sig field of the upload (section 4). The preview shows Signed or an invalid signature, and the plugin's card in the Security Dashboard keeps the result.

Things that trip people up:

  • Any change to the ZIP breaks the signature, even re-zipping the same files. Sign the exact file you distribute, and sign again for every version.
  • Only ECDSA P-256 keys are accepted, which is what cosign generate-key-pair makes. Keyless signing (Sigstore identities) and KMS references are not verified.
  • The key is read from a PEM file at startup: a missing or malformed file stops the boot instead of failing the first install. With enforce and no key, the server refuses to start.
  • With the default warn and no public key configured, nothing is verified; the server only logs a warning at startup.
  • A wrong key, a tampered ZIP and a missing .sig all read as a failed signature: under enforce, the install or the update is refused.

docs.title: 7. Resource limits and sandbox
docs.text:
Defaults applied to every plugin process:

Env var Default Effect EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE auto auto = picks best available (normally landlock). landlock = Landlock LSM allowlist + unconditional TCP egress denial (-restrict-net + seccomp -deny-inet, no carve-out for the network permission) + LD_PRELOAD seccomp. basic = LD_PRELOAD seccomp + UID drop only (debug). bubblewrap = full namespace + bind-mount root readonly + --unshare-net (also unconditional, every plugin, regardless of the network permission). strict = bubblewrap + the LD_PRELOAD seccomp shim. EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB 256 Max RSS. The resource monitor polls /proc and stops the plugin past this. 0 disables. EVEY_PLUGINS_CPU_NICE 10 nice value (0-19) applied at spawn so a plugin can never starve the server of CPU. EVEY_PLUGINS_PIDS_MAX 64 Max thread/process count. Prevents fork bombs. 0 disables. EVEY_PLUGINS_DISK_MAX_MB 100 Max install-directory size; the monitor measures it every ~30s and stops a plugin past it. 0 disables.

A plugin that talks to the network needs both permissions: [network] and external_fetch: [<host>...]. Direct network egress is cut at the sandbox for every plugin, unconditionally, regardless of its permissions (see the sandbox modes above) - the plugin process itself can never open a socket to the internet. The only way out is the host-side Fetch RPC broker: the plugin calls it over the EVEY_PLUGIN_SOCK Unix socket, the host checks the target host against external_fetch, then dials through an SSRF-safe client (private/reserved IPs rejected at connect time, redirects re-validated against both the resolved IP and the allow-listed host). See internal/adapters/driving/pluginhost/fetch.go.

docs.title: 8. Distribute a plugin
docs.text:
There is no official catalog yet: an admin installs a plugin by uploading its ZIP in the admin panel, from wherever you publish it (a GitHub release, your own site). What "distribution" means today:

  • Ship the ZIP, its .sig and your cosign.pub together (section 6), so the receiving admin can verify the upload with EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY=warn or enforce.
  • State the permissions and external_fetch hosts in your README - the admin sees them at install time and has to approve them; a surprise there is the first reason an install gets refused.
  • To have your plugin listed with the bundled examples, open a PR against examples/plugins/ with the source and a README. Examples are reviewed and built from source; a PR is not an endorsement and carries no signature from the project.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix bwrap: ... permission denied bubblewrap mode inside Docker: the default seccomp and AppArmor profiles block the unshare and mount calls it needs. Keep the default auto mode, which uses Landlock in a container. Otherwise apply the bundled profile docker/seccomp-evey.json (also in the image at /etc/evey/seccomp.json), a deliberate security downgrade: see Plugin sandbox setup. forbidden pattern "fetch(" found in theme JS Theme JS scanner caught a banned API. Themes must only call evey.theme.*. Read internal/pkg/themejs/scan.go to see what's blocked. manifest: external_fetch entry "*.tmdb.org" is a wildcard - use explicit hostnames All wildcards are rejected at install, no exceptions. Use api.tmdb.org (and list every explicit subdomain you need), not *.tmdb.org or cdn.*.tmdb.org. manifest: frontend slot "admin.section" not allowed Plugin frontends are banned from privileged areas. Pick a non-critical slot from the whitelist or rethink the plugin. signature does not match the plugin or the configured key The .sig was made with another key, or the ZIP changed after signing. Re-sign the exact ZIP with the right key, or update EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY. plugin already installed at version 1.0.0, new version must be higher The ZIP carries the version already installed. Bump version in plugin.yaml, or uninstall the plugin first. Plugin stops, the log says memory quota exceeded (… MB > … MB) The resource monitor killed it past its memory limit (exit 137). Lower memory usage, or raise the plugin's memory limit on its card in Admin → Plugins (EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB sets the default). Frontend module not visible Plugin not enabled, slot mismatch, or web_root prefix wrong in frontend.src. Check the admin Plugins page (status badge), confirm the slot string matches a real <PluginSlot name=...> mount, look at the network panel for /api/v1/plugins/{id}/assets/... calls.

docs.title: 10. Going further
docs.text:
• Security model end-to-end: security-model.md
  • Host API surface: api-reference.md
  • Available slots: api-reference.md
  • SDK code per language: sdk/
  • Reference plugins and themes: examples/plugins/

docs.title: Plugin sandboxing - which setup for your server
docs.text:
Evey runs third-party plugins inside a sandbox. For almost everyone the answer is: leave the defaults. The server detects your machine and picks the strongest isolation it can, automatically. Read on only if you run an old NAS, run Evey without Docker, or want to tighten things further.

For the full technical model see SECURITY.md. This page is the plain-language decision guide.

docs.title: What protects you (in plain words)
docs.text:
A plugin you install is boxed in. The box, depending on your machine:

  • Limits which files it can touch - it sees its own folder and the system libraries it needs to run, nothing else (not your media, not your secrets, not other plugins).
  • Blocks dangerous system actions - debugging other processes, loading kernel modules, changing the clock, mounting disks, etc. are refused at the kernel.
  • Cuts off direct network access, always. A plugin that asked for the network (and you approved it) reaches only the hosts it declared, through the server.
  • Caps CPU, memory, disk and process count, so a runaway plugin can't take the server down.
  • Keeps your secrets unreadable - the login-signing key and backups.

On top of that: plugins are admin-only to install, they're scanned for suspicious code, and you approve their permissions before they run.

Check what's actually in force: Admin → Plugins → Security Dashboard shows the host sandbox - the mode auto resolved to (landlock, bubblewrap or basic) with the individual probe results. If it shows basic, your host offers no per-path filesystem isolation (plugins run with UID-drop + seccomp only); the probes tell you why, and the sections below tell you how to fix it.

docs.title: Pick your situation
docs.text:
Your server What you get out of the box Anything to do? Modern Linux in Docker (kernel ≥ 5.13 - basically anything from ~2021 on) - the normal case Strongest isolation (Landlock), automatically. Nothing. Leave defaults. Old NAS in Docker (e.g. older Synology, kernel < 5.13) Good isolation, minus the per-folder file walls. Secrets, network and system actions are still locked down. Nothing. uid separation (below) turns itself on in this case. Any Linux, no Docker (bare-metal) Strongest isolation, automatically (Landlock on a modern kernel, otherwise bubblewrap namespaces). Follow the bare-metal guide.

How to know which one you got: open Admin → Plugins - the Security panel's badge shows the sandbox mode actually in force: landlock or bubblewrap means strong, basic means the "old NAS" case.

docs.title: The one knob you might touch: uid separation
docs.text:
What it does, plainly: makes a plugin run under a different user account than Evey itself, so it physically cannot read Evey's secret files - even if nothing else stopped it.

When it matters: only on an old machine without the per-folder file walls (i.e. the basic case). On modern machines the file walls already keep secrets out of reach, so uid separation there is just a redundant extra layer.

The setting - EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION:

Value Meaning Use it when auto (default) Turns itself on only when it's actually needed (the basic case). Off where it's redundant. Leave this - it does the right thing per machine. on Always on, even on modern machines - a second, independent secret wall on top of the file walls. You want maximum belt-and-braces and accept the small cost below. off Never. A specific plugin misbehaves when run under it (rare).

The gotcha: uid separation is incompatible with the no-new-privileges Docker hardening option - pick one. If your setup can't grant it on an old machine (basic), Evey refuses to start the plugin rather than run it next to your secrets; on a modern machine it logs a warning and runs the plugin normally (you just don't get the extra wall). The official image already ships everything needed; you only set this variable.

Small cost of on: the plugin runs as a separate account, so a plugin that writes scratch files inside its own folder could trip up. If one does, set off. (This is why the default is auto - it only takes that risk where there's a real benefit.)

docs.title: The risks, in plain words
docs.text:
What a malicious plugin could and couldn't do - by scenario:

Modern Linux (Docker or bare-metal): A bad plugin is fully boxed in. It cannot read your secrets, cannot see or touch other plugins' files, cannot make arbitrary network calls, and cannot tamper with the system. The only realistic way out is a serious Linux kernel bug - true of any sandbox that isn't a full virtual machine.

Old NAS in Docker, no per-folder walls (basic): - ✅ Your secrets stay protected (login key, backups) by the separate user account, which auto turns on here. - ✅ The plugin has no direct network; a permitted one reaches only the hosts it declared. - ✅ Dangerous system actions are still blocked at the kernel. - ⚠️ But with no per-folder walls, a bad plugin could read ordinary, non-secret files, list running processes, and - because plugins share one account - potentially read or disturb another plugin's files. - Bottom line: only install plugins you trust on such a host, or move to a modern kernel for the full file walls.

docs.title: Config examples (copy/paste)
docs.text:
These go in your .env (Docker compose) or as EVEY_* environment variables.

1. Normal modern server - recommended (do nothing): 

# Defaults are correct. Optionally make it explicit:
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=auto          # picks the strongest available
# EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=auto      # (default) on only where needed

2. Old NAS: nothing to set, auto already runs plugins under the separate account there. Keep no-new-privileges out of your compose security_opt, which would stop it: 

EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=auto
EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=auto        # (default) on in the basic case

3. Maximum belt-and-braces on a modern server (stack both walls): 

EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=auto          # → landlock
EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=on          # add the independent uid wall on top

4. Pin a specific mode (advanced): 

EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=landlock      # refuse to start plugins if Landlock is unavailable (fail-closed)

5. A plugin breaks under uid separation: 

EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=off

6. Resource caps (all admin-editable later from Admin → Plugins): 

EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB=256              # max RAM per plugin
EVEY_PLUGINS_PIDS_MAX=64                # max processes/threads
EVEY_PLUGINS_DISK_MAX_MB=100            # max install-dir size (0 = off)
EVEY_PLUGINS_CPU_NICE=10                # scheduling priority 0-19 (higher = nicer)

docs.title: Changing the sandbox mode while running
docs.text: You can change the mode from the Resource limits card on Admin → Plugins. Running plugins are restarted automatically so the new mode takes effect immediately (no manual disable/enable). The Security badge shows the mode actually in force. If a plugin can't run under the new mode (e.g. you picked bubblewrap on Docker, where it needs privileges), it shows up as errored in the dashboard - just switch back.

docs.title: Verify it's working
docs.text:
# the launcher carries the capability used for uid separation:
docker exec evey-server getcap /evey-plugin-launcher        # → cap_setuid=ep

# which user a running plugin runs as (evey = shared with server, evey-plugin = separated):
docker exec evey-server ps -o user,pid,args | grep -v grep | grep -iE "node|python"

# the sandbox mode actually in force: the Security badge on the Admin → Plugins page.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• SECURITY.md - the full plugin security model (every layer, the per-mode table, known limits).
  • deployment-bare-metal.md - running without Docker.
  • installation.md - the Docker self-host walkthrough.

docs.title: Permissions and slots
docs.text: This page is for plugin authors: what a manifest may declare, what is checked when a plugin is installed, and the rules that apply to it at run time. How the server contains a plugin, and what that containment cannot stop, is described in Security model and plugin sandbox.

docs.title: What is checked at install
docs.text:
A plugin is refused at install when:

  • kind is missing, or is neither plugin nor theme;
  • a kind: plugin lacks language or entrypoint, or a kind: theme declares them or declares permissions;
  • a permission or capability is unknown;
  • a frontend module targets a slot outside the slot list;
  • an external_fetch entry breaks the fetch rules;
  • the ZIP breaks the extraction limits: more than 5,000 files, a file over 100 MB, more than 500 MB uncompressed, a compression ratio above 100:1, a path that leaves the archive, or a symbolic link;
  • the static analysis finds a critical pattern (shell execution, obfuscation, dynamic import, sandbox escape, privilege change, mining...). Compiled binaries and embedded archives are refused unless the manifest declares native-binary.

The analysis also reads comments: a # pip install foo line in a comment is reported like real code. Remove such lines before publishing. The full list of categories is in Security model and plugin sandbox.

Before installing, the administrator sees the declared permissions, slots and hosts, and what the analysis found.

docs.title: What the plugin runs under
docs.text:
Whatever the manifest declares:

  • the plugin sees its own directory, not the server's data;
  • it has no direct network access: a plugin with the network permission reaches the hosts of its external_fetch list through the host's Fetch call;
  • without subprocess, it cannot start child processes (threads work);
  • it runs under resource limits the administrator can adjust: 256 MiB of memory, 64 processes and threads, 100 MiB of disk for its directory, and a lower CPU priority by default.

Signing is optional during development. How to sign a plugin, and the signature policy a server can enforce: Writing a plugin.

docs.title: Permissions catalog
docs.text:
A permission is declared under permissions; any other value refuses the install. Receiving webhooks (webhook.receiver) and providing metadata (metadata.provider) are capabilities, declared under capabilities: see Plugin API reference.

Permission What it grants network Plugin may make outbound network connections. Must be combined with a non-empty external_fetch list - refused at install without it. subprocess Plugin may spawn child processes. Without it, two layers apply: the LD_PRELOAD seccomp shim blocks execve/execveat for interpreted plugins, and the launcher's -deny-fork blocks process creation itself (fork/vfork/clone without CLONE_THREAD) in the kernel. Threads keep working either way. (The launcher's kernel seccomp does not deny execve - it must exec the plugin - but any child inherits the kernel filter + the Landlock domain.) native-binary Plugin may ship .so/.dll/.exe/.wasm/.jar or embedded archives. Admin sees and must accept the opaque code at install preview. filesystem Declared intent to access the filesystem beyond the plugin's own directory. Recorded and shown to the administrator; the sandbox does not grant file access outside the plugin's directory whatever is declared. media.read Plugin may call MediaRead RPCs: read media file metadata and stream access. media.write Plugin may call MediaWrite RPCs: create/update media records. api.library Plugin may call library management RPCs: list/search libraries, trigger scans. api.user Plugin may call user-scoped RPCs (read own profile, preferences). api.metadata Plugin may call metadata RPCs: search and write enrichment data. notification.sender Plugin may publish notification events (web push, email, webhook). public The plugin's interface may read a safe projection of media items (id, title, type, year, overview, poster), never paths or streams. See Plugin API reference. prefs The plugin's interface may read and write the current user's preferences in the plugin's own namespace. See Plugin API reference. hardware.gpu Highest-risk permission - admin-only, first-party tier. Grants the host's DRM render node (-render-dev, the real renderD1xx, never a card node, never /dev/dxg//dev/nvidia*//dev/kfd): a kernel-driver attack surface and a GPU-memory boundary SHARED with the transcoder (cross-process memory leak possible on AMD/Apple/Qualcomm GPUs; a hung GPU can stall transcoding). Without this permission, GPU device nodes are excluded from the Landlock device allowlist entirely (denied regardless of DAC). With it granted, the launcher adds an explicit IOCTL_DEV Landlock rule scoped to that one file (ABI v5+); on older Landlock ABIs, ioctls aren't governed by Landlock at all, so read+write access alone already permits GPU command submission. The installer surfaces a loud CRITICAL warning at preview; grant only to trusted, first-party plugins.

docs.title: External fetch rules
docs.text:
Declared in external_fetch: [...] in the manifest and checked at install by validateExternalFetch (internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner/manifest.go). All-or-nothing: one invalid entry refuses the whole install.

An entry is a bare hostname. A scheme prefix is tolerated and discarded - only the hostname is kept.

Entry Valid Reason api.tmdb.org Yes Exact hostname, the normal form https://api.tmdb.org Yes Scheme parsed and dropped, hostname kept *.tmdb.org No Wildcards are refused - list every subdomain you need * No Same rule 192.168.1.1, ::1 No IP literals are refused, both families

At run time the host broker adds its own limits, which the manifest cannot widen: http and https only, GET and HEAD only, the target host matched case-insensitively against your list, and private or reserved addresses refused after DNS resolution - redirects are re-checked against both rules.

The broker's matcher also understands a *.example.com form, but the installer refuses such an entry, so it can never reach it. Write explicit hostnames.

docs.title: Slot whitelist
docs.text:
Plugins may inject UI only in explicitly allowed slots. Critical paths are intentionally absent.

Slot Auth required Notes home.section Yes Main page content area home.hero Yes Hero banner area library.sidebar Yes Library view sidebar media.detail.sidebar Yes Media detail sidebar player.overlay Yes Player overlay UI settings.user.appearance Yes Appearance section in user settings sidebar.bottom Yes Bottom area of the navigation tray admin.nav Yes One nav entry in the admin panel opening the plugin's own sandboxed page - does not inject into existing admin screens

Never allowed: admin.* (except admin.nav), login.*, setup.*, profile.security.* - these paths are authentication/privilege-critical and plugin injection there is a privilege-escalation or phishing vector.

admin.nav content is still sandboxed like any other slot: it renders inside an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> (no allow-same-origin) with CSP default-src 'none', so it is third-party content displayed in the admin area, not an admin capability granted to the plugin.

Source: internal/domain/plugin/slots.go.

Frontend modules run in a sandboxed <iframe> with no access to the host page. The bridge limits what they can do: evey.toast at most 3 messages per second, 200 characters, no HTML; evey.navigate accepts only /home, /library, /media, /player, /settings and /search; evey.resize is clamped to 50-800 px.

docs.title: Update workflow
docs.text:
1. Admin uploads a new ZIP → PreviewPluginUpdate runs the static analyzer + cosign check and returns a diff of changed permissions/slots/external_fetch vs the installed version.
  2. If the diff is non-empty (new permissions, new slots, changed external hosts), the admin must explicitly acknowledge before the update is applied (requires_ack = true).
  3. The source hash is captured at preview and verified at apply (anti-TOCTOU: the ZIP that was analyzed is the ZIP that gets installed).
  4. If cosign policy is enforce, a signature mismatch at the apply step blocks the update even if the preview passed.

docs.title: Evey CLI - evey admin
docs.text:
The Evey server binary doubles as the operator CLI. When evey is invoked without arguments, it boots the HTTP/gRPC server; with admin as the first argument, it switches into one-shot operator mode and exits when the command completes.

All commands read configuration from the same EVEY_* env vars as the server itself (EVEY_DB_USER, EVEY_DB_PASSWORD, EVEY_DB_HOST, EVEY_DB_PORT, EVEY_DB_NAME, EVEY_DB_SSLMODE, EVEY_BACKUP_DIR, ...).

evey                          Start the server.
evey admin <subcommand>       One-shot operator tool (below). `evey admin` alone lists them,
                              `evey admin <subcommand> --help` details one.
evey version                  Version, commit, build date - needs no config or database.
evey help                     Command summary.
evey man [--text]             The manual: roff for `man`, plain text with --text.
evey completion bash          The bash completion script.

Any other first argument is refused (exit 1) rather than silently booting the server. The Go table in cmd/evey/admin_commands.go is the single description of every subcommand: the usage list, --help, the manual, the completion script and the container shell are checked against it by cmd/evey/admin_cli_test.go.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
evey admin reset-password --user <email>     Generate a new password, print it once.
evey admin rotate-jwt-key                    Regenerate JWT signing key and end every session.
evey admin restore-backup <path>             Restore the database from a .sql.gz dump (the suffix is required; not the panel's .tar.gz backups).
evey admin reindex-search [--library <id>] [--purge]   Rebuild the Meilisearch index from Postgres (--purge clears orphan docs first; if Meili is down, reports the Postgres fallback and does nothing).
evey admin migrate up [--no-backup]          Apply pending migrations.
evey admin migrate down [--no-backup]        Roll back one migration step.
evey admin migrate version                   Print current schema version (exit 1 if dirty).
evey admin list-users                        Print user emails, one per line (feeds `--user` completion).
evey admin list-libraries                    Print the library root paths, one per line (feeds `--root` completion).

docs.title: Media maintenance
docs.text:
evey admin reindex-no-cue --root <dir> [--apply] [--limit N] [--resync] [--keep-backup=false]
                                             Rebuild the seek index (Cues) of MKV/WebM files that
                                             lack one - the fix for slow seek and slow resume.
                                             DRY-RUN BY DEFAULT: pass --apply to rewrite. Each
                                             rewrite is validated, cross-checked, and keeps a
                                             .mkvgobak backup. --limit N for a cautious first run.
                                             --resync also repairs files with a corrupted region the
                                             strict pass refuses (skips the damage, keeps the rest,
                                             reports the lost bytes).
                                             LONG: rewrites each file in full, hours on a large
                                             library. Shows a progress bar while applying.
evey admin validate-streaming --root <dir> [--errors-only]
                                             Read-only report of each file's streaming readiness
                                             (Cues index, keyframe cues, DefaultDuration) - what the
                                             on-demand HLS rung and seeking rely on.
evey admin artwork-gc [--root <dir>] [--apply]
                                             Delete artwork files on disk that no DB row references.
                                             Dry-run by default. --root defaults to /data/artworks.
evey admin reclassify <media-id>             Force-recompute the encoding complexity class.
evey admin reclassify --all                  Wipe and re-queue every classified item.

docs.title: Diagnostics and capacity
docs.text:
evey admin doctor [--repair]                 Health-check DB, schema, jwt.key, Meilisearch (plus
                                             index drift), media mounts (owned by the server UID?),
                                             cache dirs, ffmpeg/mkvgo and disk. --repair applies only
                                             the safe fixes (create + chown missing writable dirs).
evey admin rollback                          Read-only advisor: prints the running version, schema,
                                             newest pre-migration backup and the exact HOST commands
                                             to roll back. The container has no Docker access, by
                                             design, so it advises rather than acts.
evey admin load-test [minimal|standard|max] [--scenario <s>] [--mode <m>] [--max-viewers N] [--duration S] [--cold-cache]
                                             Needs a LIVE server (it is an HTTP client of the local
                                             gateway). Ramps simulated viewers until the box hits its
                                             ceiling, then reports the sustained count with TTFF and
                                             segment latencies. Scenarios: transcode, natural, mkvgo,
                                             light (80/20), balanced (50/50, default), heavy (20/80),
                                             mkvgo+N. --max-viewers caps the ramp (0 = server default
                                             12). Short sanity run:
                                             `load-test --scenario balanced --max-viewers 4`.
                                             `admission_full` is the ceiling verdict (exit 0), not an
                                             error.
evey admin route-bench [--backend nvenc|vaapi|qsv|none] [--heights ...] [--fps ...] [--out rows.csv] [--json run.json] [<file>...]
                                             Measure what a session of each transcode route costs on
                                             this host against the calibration and the admission cost
                                             model. Minutes of full load; never while serving.
evey admin ladder-bench [--scenes 3] [--window 8] [--heights ...] [--crf ...] [--out rows.csv] <file>...
                                             Ladder complexity features on a few scenes per title,
                                             encoded at fixed CRFs and scored. Never while serving.
evey admin ladder-probe [--window 8] [--cache <dir>] [--out <dir>] <file>...
                                             Per-title probe timing and early-stop rate on the files.

docs.title: Demo instance
docs.text:
evey admin demo-seed [--apply] [--media]     Run the demo bootstrap by hand: the demo administrator,
                                             the visitor accounts, the four libraries, and with
                                             --media the freely licensed media (gigabytes). Refuses
                                             unless EVEY_DEMO=1. Dry-run by default.

The full, always-current list is evey admin with no subcommand: it prints every subcommand the binary carries.

docs.title: In the container (standard installation)
docs.text:
docker exec evey-server evey admin doctor
docker exec -it evey-server bash      # an admin shell: evey admin ..., man evey

The image sets the database password file, so the commands reach the embedded database without any extra environment.

docs.title: On a bare-metal install (no Docker)
docs.text:
evey admin reset-password --user alice@example.com
evey admin migrate version

The pre-installed binary already has every subcommand built in.

docs.title: On the development stack
docs.text:
The Makefile wraps the migration commands, which run from the source tree in the evey-server dev container:

make migrate-version
make migrate-up
make migrate-down

docs.title: Tab-completion and the manual
docs.text:
The binary carries its own bash completion and manual, so both always match the subcommands it ships:

evey completion bash | sudo tee /etc/bash_completion.d/evey >/dev/null
evey man | sudo tee /usr/local/share/man/man1/evey.1 >/dev/null && sudo mandb -q

zsh users: autoload -U +X bashcompinit && bashcompinit first, then source the same script. Completion covers the subcommands, their flags and flag values (--mode, --backend, --scenario), user emails after --user, the library roots the server knows after --root (plus any directory), media files only for the file arguments of ladder-bench, ladder-probe and route-bench, and .sql.gz dumps for restore-backup.

The Docker image installs the completion at build time and its admin shell (docker exec -it evey-server bash) answers man evey by paging evey man --text, since the image ships no man binary.

docs.title: migrate
docs.text:
• up applies every pending migration in order. A pre-migration pg_dump is taken automatically when EVEY_BACKUP_DIR is set (default in the Docker image: /data/backups). Failure mid-Up leaves schema_migrations.dirty = true; see migration-runbook.md.
  • down rolls back exactly one migration. Surgical, not "tear it all down" - there's no down --all. Also takes a pre-rollback pg_dump.
  • version prints the current schema version. Returns exit code 1 with a DIRTY warning when a previous migration failed halfway (i.e. some but not all Up statements ran).
  • --no-backup skips the pg_dump for either direction. Useful on hosts without postgres-client installed (typical WSL dev path where the Makefile already passes the flag).

docs.title: reset-password, rotate-jwt-key, restore-backup, reindex-search
docs.text: See docs/runbooks/recovery.md for the full procedure, prerequisites, and post-conditions.

docs.title: What's not in evey admin
docs.text:
Three standalone binaries live next to cmd/evey because they're not operator commands in the recovery / schema sense:

Binary Purpose Why standalone cmd/intro-backfill Refresh intro detection on a slice of the catalog after a pipeline change API client - talks to /api/v1/admin/media/{id}/detect-segments with a bearer token, not in-process. cmd/intro-diag Diagnose why pHash intro detection matched (or didn't) on a specific series Developer debug tool - reads trickplay sprites off disk, prints a frame-by-frame Hamming match map. Optional audio cross-correlation pass. cmd/trickplay-verify Verify that each trickplay tile actually shows the frame at the recorded timestamp QA/CI tool - re-extracts source frames via ffmpeg and aHashes them against the tile.

They're shipped as separate binaries because none of them needs the full server config plumbing - they're scoped, run-once tools, not part of the recovery surface.

docs.title: Related runbooks
docs.text:
• migration-runbook.md - schema deploy, rollback, dirty-state recovery.
  • recovery.md - password reset, JWT key rotation, backup restore, search reindex.
  • incident-runbook.md - first-response when the server is misbehaving.

docs.title: Incident Runbook
docs.text:
First-response playbook for common Evey outages. Each section: symptom → diagnose → fix.

The commands target the standard installation: one container, evey-server, with Postgres and Meilisearch running inside it; their logs are the postgres: and Meilisearch lines of docker logs evey-server. The repository's docker-compose.yml layout adds evey-postgres and evey-caddy containers (Advanced deployments).

To run SQL against the embedded database:

docker exec evey-server sh -c \
  'PGPASSWORD=$(cat /data/keys/postgres.password) psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U evey evey'

Default HTTP port: 9091 (EVEY_HTTP_PORT). Health endpoint: /healthz.

Logs. Two copies of the same stream: the daily file evey-data/logs/evey-YYYY-MM-DD.log (EVEY_LOG_DIR, /data/logs inside the image) and docker logs evey-server. The file is authoritative: the json-file driver rotates docker logs, and after a rotation the command can stop hours before the container did - a load test's stop_detail or a calibration verdict then looks missing when it is only rotated away. When they disagree, read the file, or as root the raw /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/*-json.log* files. The docker logs one-liners below assume a recent, unrotated window.

docs.title: 1. Server not reachable
docs.text:
Symptom: clients fail to connect; curl http://localhost:9091/healthz times out or returns connection refused.

Diagnose: 

docker ps --filter name=evey-server
docker logs --tail=200 evey-server
docker inspect --format='{{.State.Health.Status}}' evey-server
ss -ltnp | grep 9091                # port actually listening?
curl -v http://localhost:9091/healthz

Common causes + fix: - Container exited → docker logs evey-server for the panic, fix, docker compose up -d evey. - Healthcheck failing because DB or Meili is down → see sections 4 and 5. - Port clash on host → change EVEY_HTTP_PORT or free the port. - Caddy in front not routing → docker logs evey-caddy, verify EVEY_DOMAIN and that evey healthcheck is green (Caddy depends on it).

docs.title: 2. All logins return 401
docs.text:
Symptom: every user - including admins who logged in yesterday - gets 401 from /api/v1/auth/*.

Diagnose: 

docker logs --since 10m evey-server | grep -iE 'epoch|jwt|auth|signing|private key'
docker exec evey-server ls -l /data/jwt.key

Look for the epoch line first. Every authenticated request re-checks the user's token epoch against the database (ADR-0019), and that check fails CLOSED. So a database that is slow, locked or unreachable makes every request in the server return the same 401 an expired token returns - which reads exactly like a JWT problem and is not one. The server says so explicitly:

auth rejected: the token epoch could not be read, so every authenticated
request is failing - check the database, not the JWT key

If that line is present, stop reading this section and go to §4 (database). /healthz can still be green here: it only pings the connection, it does not run the epoch query. The Prometheus counter is evey_auth_failures_total{reason="epoch_lookup_failed"}.

Common causes + fix: - JWT key missing or changed is rarely the cause. An unreadable or corrupted EVEY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH (default /data/jwt.key) stops the server from starting; a missing one is regenerated. Access tokens signed by the old key are then refused, but the apps renew them with their refresh token, which is checked in the database, not against the key: users stay signed in. Confirm the evey-data volume is mounted at /data: without it the database is missing too. - Rate limit tripping every request: check EVEY_RATELIMIT_LOGIN_MAX (default 10 per IP per minute) and EVEY_RATELIMIT_GLOBAL_MAX (default 300). Reverse proxy forwarding all traffic as a single IP will trip this fast - add the proxy to Trusted proxies in Admin → Remote Access (applies without a restart; EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES also works). Dev override already sets 1000 / 10000. - Clock skew between server and clients → date -u on the host.

docs.title: 3. Transcoding fails / videos won't play transcoded
docs.text:
Symptom: playback works for direct play, fails when a transcode is required. Player errors, server logs show ffmpeg exit codes.

Diagnose: 

docker exec evey-server which ffmpeg ffprobe
docker exec evey-server ffmpeg -version | head -1
docker logs --since 10m evey-server | grep -iE 'ffmpeg|transcode|hls'
docker exec evey-server ls -ld /cache/transcode /data/trickplay
docker exec evey-server df -h /cache

Common causes + fix: - ffmpeg binary missing (custom image without it): rebuild from the official Dockerfile. - Cache dir not writable: EVEY_TRANSCODING_CACHE_DIR defaults to /data/transcode in code but compose maps it to /cache/transcode via the evey-cache named volume. EVEY_TRICKPLAY_CACHE_DIR is /data/trickplay in the image (/cache/trickplay is the default outside it). Verify writability: 

docker exec evey-server touch /cache/transcode/.write-test && \
  docker exec evey-server rm /cache/transcode/.write-test
- Cache full → see section 6. - Hardware acceleration misbehaving: set Hardware acceleration to Off in Admin → Transcoding → Encode calibration (applies live, re-measures) to keep every transcode on the processor, and confirm the problem is hardware-related before switching back to Auto. - "The server is busy transcoding other streams": the live capacity is measured, not set; see Transcoding and server capacity. EVEY_TRANSCODING_MAX_CONCURRENT (Max Concurrent in Admin → Transcode Cache) only covers transcode jobs outside live playback.

docs.title: 3c. "It buffers / it cut out" and the logs do not say why
docs.text:
Symptom: a viewer reports stalls or dropouts on a transcoded title, and the server logs show hls-vod: segment timeout with err:"context canceled" - which means the CLIENT hung up, not that the server timed out.

Diagnose: the server already records every decision it made. Start there, because it is free:

# Why a segment request reused an encoder or spawned one, and what it cost the
# player. Only logged when it costs something: a wait beyond one segment, or a
# spawn. `over_client_patience: true` is the smoking gun.
docker exec evey-server grep '"software: reach decision"' /data/logs/evey-$(date +%F).log | tail -40

# The encoders themselves: spawns, kills and their reason.
docker exec evey-server grep -E '"software: session (started|killed)"|per-hash cap' \
  /data/logs/evey-$(date +%F).log | tail -40

Those lines say what the server decided. When you need what ffmpeg actually achieved second by second - the frontier's real position over time - turn on the per-encoder progress recording:

# ON. Applies to the NEXT encoder; no restart needed. $TOKEN is an admin JWT.
curl -sf -X PUT http://localhost:9091/api/v1/admin/server-config/transcode.ffmpeg_progress_log \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"value":"true"}'

# Reproduce the problem, then read one session: out_time = content produced so
# far, speed = how far ahead of real time the encoder ran.
docker exec evey-server ls -t /data/logs/ffmpeg | head
docker exec evey-server tail -20 /data/logs/ffmpeg/<file>.log

# OFF again when you are done.
curl -sf -X PUT http://localhost:9091/api/v1/admin/server-config/transcode.ffmpeg_progress_log \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"value":"false"}'

Leave it off outside an investigation. It is one file per encoder, a few MB per session, written for every playback on the box - real disk and real writes on a weak NAS. The file name carries the decision hash, the rung (-vN-) and the start segment (-sN-), so it lines up with the JSON log above; a respawn at the same position gets its own file rather than overwriting the previous run, which is what makes encoder churn visible.

Common causes + fix: - Repeated short forward seeks: each one may spawn a fresh encoder, and the per-hash cap (MaxSessionsPerHash, default 2) evicts the least recently used one. Expect session killed reason:lru_cap in the log. Normal in moderation. - The client is less patient than the server: clientSegmentPatience (6 s) is what the seek-reach window is sized against; AndroidX Media3 abandons a segment at ~8 s while the server's WaitBudgetDur is 60 s. A reach decision line with over_client_patience: true means the server was about to ask for a wait no player would sit through.

docs.title: 3b. stale_rendition 410s / player refetches its master mid-play
docs.text:
Symptom: player briefly stalls then recovers; logs show hls-vod: stale rendition URL refused (the ladder moved under a live player) and requests answered 410 Gone with X-Evey-Error: stale_rendition.

What it means: this is a protection firing, not the failure itself. Every manifest URI carries the decision hash it was built under (fp=). A 410 means a player presented a URL from a session whose ABR ladder has since been reshaped - serving it would hand the decoder bytes from a different rendition (the "rainbow screen" incident class, ADR 0022 §1b). The refusal forces a clean master refetch instead.

Diagnose: the WARN carries sealed_fp vs current_fp and the media id. - A burst right after a deploy/restart or an admin recalibration is expected: live sessions outlived a capability change. No action; players resync within one poll. - A steady drip during normal operation means something keeps reshaping ladders under live streams - look for capability flapping (docker logs evey-server | grep -iE 'calibrat|capability'), an admission shaper churning under load, or a CMCD cap override oscillating. - Players that loop on 410 without recovering are holding a cached master (old app build, aggressive proxy caching of .m3u8). Verify the proxy does not cache manifests (Cache-Control: no-cache must pass through).

docs.title: 4. Database connection refused / errors
docs.text:
Symptom: server logs contain dial tcp ... connect: connection refused, pq: ..., or queries time out.

Diagnose: 

docker logs --tail=300 evey-server | grep -iE 'postgres|database'
docker exec evey-server sh -c 'PGPASSWORD=$(cat /data/keys/postgres.password) psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U evey evey -c "
  SELECT count(*), state
    FROM pg_stat_activity
   WHERE datname = current_database()
   GROUP BY state;"'
df -h ./evey-data

Common causes + fix: - Disk full under ./evey-data (the database lives in ./evey-data/postgres) → free space, then docker compose restart evey. - Pool exhausted (too many connections or long waits) → EVEY_DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS (default 25). Kill stuck sessions: 

SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)
  FROM pg_stat_activity
 WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
   AND now() - state_change > interval '5 minutes';
- Separate Postgres container (repository layout): docker ps --filter name=evey-postgres, docker logs --tail=200 evey-postgres; the server's EVEY_DB_USER / EVEY_DB_PASSWORD / EVEY_DB_NAME must match the postgres service.

docs.title: 5. Meilisearch down
docs.text:
Symptom: search returns degraded results, logs show meilisearch unavailable, using SQL search fallback.

Behavior: search keeps working through SQL (cmd/evey/wire.go wires a resilient search adapter that logs that line when Meilisearch is unreachable). No user action is needed to stay online; only ranking quality degrades.

Meilisearch runs inside evey-server (EVEY_EMBEDDED_MEILI, on by default), listening on 127.0.0.1:7700 in the container only.

Diagnose + fix: 

docker exec evey-server curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:7700/health
docker logs --tail=300 evey-server | grep -i meili
- Unhealthy → docker compose restart evey. - Index corrupted → stop the container, move ./evey-data/meili aside, start again, then rebuild the index from the database: docker exec evey-server evey admin reindex-search.

docs.title: 6. Transcode cache disk full
docs.text:
Symptom: transcodes fail with no space left on device; container healthcheck flaps.

Diagnose: 

docker exec evey-server df -h /cache
docker exec evey-server du -sh /cache/transcode /data/trickplay 2>/dev/null
docker volume inspect evey_evey-cache   # compose-mangled name may vary

Fix: - Safe purge - the cache is regenerable: 

docker exec evey-server sh -c 'rm -rf /cache/transcode/*'
This also drops photos/ (resized photo variants) and track-art/ (a track's tag-embedded cover, extracted once and resized) under it - both are rebuilt on the next request. Clear All in Admin → Transcode Cache does the same purge. - Trickplay is more expensive to regenerate; only purge if necessary: 
docker exec evey-server sh -c 'rm -rf /data/trickplay/*'
- Lower the Transcode cache budget (Admin → Server Config → Server Settings, default 10 GB) if the host volume is tight; whatever the budget, the sweeper keeps 2 GiB free on the cache volume.

docs.title: 7. Plugin crashed
docs.text:
Symptom: a plugin stops responding; server logs show panics from plugin runner.

Diagnose: 

docker logs --since 30m evey-server 2>&1 | grep -iE 'plugin|pluginrunner|panic'
# Look for: "panic in plugin runner", "plugin process crashed", "remove plugin sock on crash"

Fix: - Try a surgical restart first, no container downtime: POST /api/v1/admin/plugins/<id>/enable. This works even when the plugin is already enabled but stuck in Error status - StartPlugin's guard relaunches it as soon as the status is not Running. Prefer this over restarting the whole server, especially when SSH access to the host is not readily available. - If the surgical restart does not clear it, disable the offending plugin from the admin panel instead. - If the server itself is unstable, restart: docker compose restart evey. - Inspect plugin files at ./evey-data/plugins/ (host) == /data/plugins (container). Remove the broken plugin zip/dir, restart. - Send the panic trace + plugin id to the plugin author.

docs.title: 8. A cast froze, went silent, or the phone keeps spinning
docs.text:
Everything below is readable from the admin Logs page (or GET /api/v1/admin/logs/search?q=<term>&limit=200): no shell on the box is needed. Times are UTC. Every beacon is a player-client: playback event reported line with type= and a details= string. Credentials never appear in what these routes return (bearers, JWTs and token=/password= values read [redacted]), so a cast URL's token is not something a log search can recover - grep for the media id, not the token.

  1. Was the receiver alive, and until when? Search cast_receiver_alive. The receiver posts one every 30 s while it plays; details carries buf=<behind>/<ahead>/<ranges> (seconds buffered behind and ahead of the playhead) and pos_sec. Healthy playback shows ahead in the tens of seconds. The last beacon's time is when the receiver died or was killed: nothing after it means the television is no longer running the receiver, whatever the phone shows.
  2. Why did it stop? Search cast_receiver_finished: reason=INTERRUPTED is a new LOAD replacing the running one (look for a StartStream a few seconds earlier), reason=ERROR carries the player error. No finished at all after the last alive = the receiver process disappeared (a Chromecast HD killed for memory on a 20+ Mbps copy master, most often).
  3. What did the phone see? Search cast_sender_stall: the sender posts state=playing frozen=<n>s pos=<p> when the Cast SDK still says PLAYING but the position has not moved for 20 s, and state=idle reason=<r> when the receiver reported an idle reason. These lines are logged at WARN, so the admin Logs page's warning filter surfaces them. This is the sender's side of the same minute - compare its pos with the receiver's last pos_sec.
  4. Did the session cascade? Search refresh rejected: a refresh token "not found" logs the app out and back in (saved credentials), which re-issues the stream - the line now says the token's jti, issued and age, which tells a stale copy from a forged one. Search StartStream to see re-issues; the sender no longer re-loads the receiver on a re-issued URL for the same title.
  5. Was the stream too big for the device? Search advertises a fallback rung (the copy master's peak bitrate) and plan fitted to the client's line (the receiver's maxKbps measure or its abr=floor rescue, now a plan input - the transcode master that follows carries the reason client_line_exceeded or abr_floor_requested): a session that started on a 20+ Mbps copy master and fell to a fitted 1080p rung after a few seconds is the floor rescue doing its job; a re-LOAD that starts again on the copy master is the pattern that kills a Chromecast HD.
  6. Server-side starvation? Search on-demand resource refused: a burst of context canceled refusals on consecutive segments is a scrub (each request cancelled by the next), not a server fault; served lines with long durations are.

If steps 1-3 show the receiver alive and the sender silent, the problem is in the phone's Cast session (the SDK, the network to the TV); if the receiver's beacons stop first, the television is where to look (memory, codec, the stream's bitrate).

docs.title: Kill a compromised session / device
docs.text:
Symptom: admin sees an unexpected device in Now Playing (admin panel), or a user reports an unknown device in their session list.

  1. Identify the session_id: 
    docker exec evey-server sh -c 'PGPASSWORD=$(cat /data/keys/postgres.password) psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U evey evey -c "
  SELECT id, profile_id, device_name, client_ip, started_at
  FROM play_sessions
  WHERE ended_at IS NULL
  ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 20;"'
  2. Kill from admin UI: Admin → Now Playing, the stop icon on the session (Stop session), then Stop to confirm; or via gRPC AdminSessionService/KillSession with the session_id. The session is terminated 5s later so the player can receive the stop command.
  3. If the stream keeps running anyway, restart the container: every encoder stops with it. 
    docker compose restart evey
  4. If the account itself is compromised, Admin → Users → Disable on it: that deletes its refresh tokens and invalidates its access tokens at once, so every device is signed out. Set a new password (evey admin reset-password --user <email>, which also ends the account's sessions), then Enable the account again.

docs.title: Unblock a stuck library scan
docs.text:
Symptom: a library scan shows "in progress" for hours but no file progress in logs.

  1. Check whether the scan still logs anything - if the process is hung, CPU is idle and recent logs show no scan: line: 
    docker logs --tail=500 evey-server | grep 'scan:'
  2. A scan lock is in-memory (no DB row), so a server restart clears it: 
    docker compose restart evey
  3. If a specific file is causing repeated panics (see stack traces), quarantine it by moving it out of the library path, then re-scan.
  4. If inotify watches are exhausted (kernel limit), bump: 
    echo fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288 | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf
sudo sysctl -p

docs.title: General diagnostic cheatsheet
docs.text:
# Status of everything
docker compose ps
curl -sf http://localhost:9091/healthz && echo healthy

# Tail every container
docker compose logs --tail=100 -f

# Server config dump
docker exec evey-server env | grep ^EVEY_ | sort

# Database size
docker exec evey-server sh -c 'PGPASSWORD=$(cat /data/keys/postgres.password) psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U evey evey -c "
  SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(current_database()));"'

# Host disk
df -h ./evey-data

docs.title: Media health
docs.text:
Admin → Media Health reads every MKV/WebM file of your libraries and gives each one a single answer. The aim is a page that empties out: what Evey can fix, it fixes; the rest is mentioned once and can be marked as seen.

A scan with one file Evey can repair (its seek index is missing) and one remark (surplus bytes after the end of the file, harmless).

docs.title: Three verdicts
docs.text:
Verdict What it means What Evey does Healthy Index, container, sizes and audio timing check out. Nothing. Repairable here A defect Evey repairs on this server. Repair all handles them in the background. Information Something measured about the file that Evey does not rewrite on its own. Nothing. Mark it as seen.

None of them hands you a chore. A measurement Evey cannot act on is a remark, and a measurement can be wrong: if the file plays fine, it is fine.

docs.title: Repairable here
docs.text:
• Missing seek index, or one that cannot be used. The symptom is a slow seek or a slow resume. The index is rebuilt in a temporary copy, the copy is checked in full (tracks, duration, index), then it replaces the file.
  • Wrong container: the .mkv is really an MP4 or MOV file. It is renamed to .mp4 and the library follows; nothing is rewritten.
  • Damaged stretch: a corrupted region in the middle of the file. The repair skips it and resynchronises what follows, so those bytes are lost for good. The repair dialog asks for it explicitly (Also resync N damaged files); left unticked, damaged files are not touched. The same applies to a file whose corruption only appears while it is rewritten (Corruption found during repair): the scan reads headers only and could not see it.
  • Tracks stored in blocks: minutes of video, then minutes of audio, instead of side by side. No player gets past the first block. Re-mux the tracks rewrites them side by side without re-encoding and checks that every packet made it before replacing the file.

docs.title: Information
docs.text:
• Incomplete download: the end of the file never arrived. It plays up to the cut. No tool recovers the missing part; only the source does.
  • Coarse seeking: the rebuilt index still has a hole, most often the final credits. A seek into the hole lands at its edge; everywhere else seeking is exact.
  • Audio at +N s: an audio track starts after the picture. This is how a dub is lined up with a cut, and every player follows it. Evey never rewrites it.
  • Audio tracks N s apart: the file's own audio tracks disagree, so one of them is in the wrong place. Nothing measured can tell which one.
  • Sound N s off the picture: an audio track is away from where the subtitles, timed to the picture, place the speech.
  • Audio track pulled to 0: the mark an earlier repair leaves when it pulled a track back by its declared delay. If the dub now plays early, the removed amount is no longer in the file.
  • Audio -N s: an audio track ends before the picture. Playback fills the gap with silence.
  • Trailing bytes: surplus bytes after the end of the file's content. It plays fine.
  • Unreadable: the scan could not read the file (missing, unreadable, or a container the parser refused). Check the mount or the source.

docs.title: Checking the sync by eye
docs.text:
For the three audio remarks, Check sync on the file's row builds a short clip on the server: pick a moment, a track and an offset to try, then watch it, slowed down if needed. Comparing tracks says whether they agree, never which one follows the picture; only watching settles it.

Apply N s to this track moves that track by the chosen offset. The change is recorded as your judgement, not as a measurement, and History can undo it.

docs.title: Marking as seen
docs.text:
Seen, stop flagging (one file) and Mark all as seen (a group) take an Information remark out of the Awaiting view. Only remarks can be marked: a repairable defect gets repaired. The mark belongs to the file as it is: if its size or date changes, the next scan diagnoses it again. Flag again undoes the mark.

The views above the table (Awaiting, Repairable, Info, Seen, Backups, All) and the search box are how you work through a large library: Awaiting is the to-do list.

docs.title: Scans
docs.text:
A scan reads the head of each file (a few kilobytes) and reuses the previous answer for a file that has not changed. Disk use sets the pace:

  • Discreet: one file at a time, then a pause as long as the read took. The disks stay free about half the time, so someone can keep watching.
  • Fast: several files at once, no pause. About three times quicker on a library spread over several disks, but playback may stutter meanwhile.

Two things make a scan diagnose everything again: a file that changed, and a new version of Evey whose checks changed. The first scan after such an update is therefore long on a large library; the following ones are quick again.

docs.title: Backups, history and undo
docs.text:
Keep backups is on by default: every rewritten file keeps its original as a .mkvgobak next to it. Roll back restores one file, Roll back all the selected scope, and Delete backups removes them for good. Turned off, only the last few copies exist during a run and they are removed at its end; each repair is then verified more deeply before it replaces the file. When keeping a copy of every file would fill the volume, the page says so before the run.

The Repair journal lists every change a repair made to a file's bytes, across the library; History shows it for one file. Some changes can be undone from there without any copy:

Change Undo Audio track moved Applies the exact opposite shift. Renamed to .mp4 Renames it back. Index rebuilt Nothing to undo: picture and sound are untouched. Damaged stretch skipped Only the backup brings the lost bytes back, which is why this repair always keeps one. After Repair all: the index is rebuilt, the journal records it, and the file leaves the queue; the remark stays. This index was patched into the file in place, which keeps no copy: only a file that has to be rewritten keeps a backup.

Repairs write into your media folders. They must be mounted read-write in the container (no :ro on the volume); after a run that met a read-only volume, the page says so. Scanning works either way.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
The same engine is available from the operator CLI (see cli.md):

  • evey admin reindex-no-cue --root <dir> [--apply] [--resync] rebuilds the missing indexes, as a dry run unless --apply is given;
  • evey admin validate-streaming --root <dir> prints the read-only streaming readiness report.

docs.title: Database migrations
docs.text: How Evey changes its database schema during an update, and what to do when it goes wrong. The commands target the standard installation, where the database runs inside the evey-server container.

docs.title: How migrations run
docs.text:
The migrations are embedded in the binary (go:embed) and applied by golang-migrate when the server starts (internal/adapters/driven/postgres/migrate.go, files internal/adapters/driven/postgres/migrations/NNNNNN_<name>.{up,down}.sql). The state is the schema_migrations table: {version, dirty}.

Before applying anything, the server writes a full dump to /data/backups/pre-migration-<version>-<time>.sql.gz (EVEY_BACKUP_DIR). The newest dump of each of the 3 most recent schema versions is kept.

The same operations are available by hand:

docker exec evey-server evey admin migrate version   # exit 1 when the schema is dirty
docker exec evey-server evey admin migrate up
docker exec evey-server evey admin migrate down      # exactly one step

up and down also take a dump first; --no-backup skips it.

To run SQL against the embedded database:

docker exec evey-server sh -c \
  'PGPASSWORD=$(cat /data/keys/postgres.password) psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U evey evey'

docs.title: Before an update
docs.text:
1. Take a backup in Admin → Database Backup (Run now), or from a script: 

    curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>" \
  http://localhost:9091/api/v1/admin/backups
    The automatic pre-migration dump is a second copy, not a replacement.

  2. For a large catalogue, look at the size of the biggest tables: a migration that rewrites one of them takes longer. 

    SELECT relname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) AS total,
       n_live_tup
  FROM pg_stat_user_tables
 ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC
 LIMIT 20;

  3. Check the current version: evey admin migrate version. If it reports a dirty schema, see A migration that stopped halfway first.

docs.title: Running the migrations
docs.text:
They run when the new image starts:

docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
docker logs -f evey-server

The container reports healthy once the migrations are applied and the server answers:

curl -sf http://localhost:9091/healthz && echo OK
docker exec evey-server evey admin migrate version

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
evey admin rollback prints the running version, the schema version, the newest pre-migration dump and the exact commands to run on the host. It changes nothing: the container has no access to Docker.

The usual way back is the previous image with the dump taken before the update: see Going back in Backups and updates. evey admin migrate down rolls back one step at a time instead, when the .down.sql of that step is enough.

Do not edit schema_migrations by hand, except to clear a dirty state (below), and take a dump first.

Restore the pre-migration dump rather than migrating down when the update dropped data (a removed column, a type change).

docs.title: A migration that stopped halfway
docs.text:
If the log shows Dirty database version N. Fix and force version., a migration crashed partway. Bring the schema to the state you want, then clear the flag:

SELECT version, dirty FROM schema_migrations;

-- Re-apply the rest of the up.sql by hand, or revert with the down.sql,
-- then record the version you actually reached:
UPDATE schema_migrations SET version = <N>, dirty = false;

Restart the container; the migrations continue from there. Restoring the pre-migration dump is the other way out.

docs.title: Writing a migration
docs.text:
For contributors. Examples in internal/adapters/driven/postgres/migrations/:

  • 000066_cascade_and_email_unique.up.sql - ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY. Takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on both tables for the duration of the ADD. Cheap on small tables, painful on media_items / watch_progress. Pattern for large tables: add with NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a second statement (validate only takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE).
  • 000067_sort_title_index.up.sql, 000068_watch_progress_composite_index.up.sql, 000069_quick_connect_shortcode_index.up.sql - plain CREATE INDEX. On large tables this locks writes. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a migrate transaction.
  • 000072_syncplay_queue.up.sql - ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]'. On PG 11+ this is metadata-only and fast. Still holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE briefly.

Guidelines:

  • Long ALTER that rewrites the table (type change, adding a non-constant default on old PG) → expect downtime on a large catalogue.
  • DROP COLUMN → only metadata, but the column cannot be restored without a backup. Never drop it in the same release as the code that stops reading it - prefer a two-step: stop reading the column, deploy, then drop in the next release.
  • FK on big tables → ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a follow-up migration. Avoid a single blocking ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY ....
  • Batch UPDATE / backfill → never in a single migration on a big table. Ship a no-op schema migration + a background job.
  • Column replacement (expand → migrate → contract) → do not fold ADD COLUMN + backfill + SET NOT NULL + DROP COLUMN of the old one into a single migration. That shape only works because Evey runs single-instance today, with migrations applied synchronously at boot: during the window, old code reading the dropped column and new code reading the new one cannot coexist, so a rolling or multi-replica deploy would serve errors from whichever half is behind.
